American actress, dancer, painter, and poet (1835–1868)

| Born | (1835-06-15)June 15, 1835 |

**Adah Isaacs Menken** (June 15, 1835–August 10, 1868) was an American actress, painter and poet, and was the highest earning actress of her time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) She was best known for her performance in the [hippodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippodrama "Hippodrama")_[Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural\_legacy\_of\_Mazeppa#The\_1830s-1860s "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa")_, with a climax that featured her apparently nude and riding a horse on stage. After great success for a few years with the play in New York and San Francisco, she appeared in a production in London and Paris, from 1864 to 1866. After a brief trip back to the United States, she returned to Europe. She became ill within two years and died in Paris at the age of 33.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-2)

Menken told many versions of her origins, including her name, place of birth, ancestry, and religion, and historians have differed in their accounts. Most have said she was born a [Louisiana Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people") Catholic, with European and African ancestry. A celebrity who created sensational performances in the United States and Europe, she married several times and was also known for her affairs. She had two sons, both of whom died in infancy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-3)

Though she was better known as an actress, Menken sought to be known as a writer. She published about 20 essays, 100 poems, and a book of her collected poems, from 1855 to 1868 (the book was published posthumously). Early work was devoted to family and after her marriage, her poetry and essays featured Jewish themes. Beginning with work published after moving to New York, with which she changed her style, Menken expressed a wide range of emotions and ideas about women's place in the world. Her collection _Infelicia_ went through several editions and was in print until 1902.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Accounts of Menken's early life and origins vary considerably. In her autobiographical "Some Notes of Her Life in Her Own Hand," published in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ in 1868, Menken said she was born in [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), and lived in [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba") as a child before her family settled in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"). There are many conflicting reports as to Menken's birth name, but she has been called Marie Rachel Adelaide de Vere Spenser and Adah Bertha Theodore, and Ed James, a journalist friend, wrote after her death: "Her real name was Adelaide McCord, and she was born at [Milneburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milneburg "Milneburg"), near New Orleans, on June 15, 1835."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4) Menken's birth year also varies, with some records stating 1835 and some stating 1832.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Notes-5) Elsewhere, in 1865, she wrote that her birth name was Dolores Adios Los Fiertes, and that she was the daughter of a French woman from New Orleans and a [Spanish-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Jews "Spanish Jews") man.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) About 1940, the consensus of scholars was that her parents were Auguste Théodore, a [free Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_black "Free black") man, and Marie, a [mixed-race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-race "Mixed-race") Creole, and Adah was raised as a Catholic. She had a sister and a brother.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)

Based on Menken's assertions of being a native of New Orleans, [Wolf Mankowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Mankowitz "Wolf Mankowitz") and others have studied Board of Health records for the city. They have concluded that Ada was born in the city as the legitimate daughter of Auguste Théodore, a [free man of color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_people_of_color "Free people of color") (mixed race) and his wife Magdaleine Jean Louis Janneaux,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-7) likely also a [Louisiana Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people"). Ada would have been raised as Catholic. However, in 1990, John Cofran, using census records, said that she was born as Ada C. McCord, in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), in late 1830. He said she was the daughter of an Irish merchant, Richard McCord, and his wife Catherine.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) According to Cofran, her father died when she was young and her mother remarried. The family then moved from Memphis to New Orleans.

Menken was said to have been a bright student; she became fluent in French and Spanish,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) and was described as having a gift for languages.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) As a child, Menken performed as a dancer in the ballet of the [French Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Opera_House "French Opera House") in New Orleans. In her later childhood, she performed as a dancer in [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"), [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), where she was crowned "Queen of the Plaza."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

## American career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: American career")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg/250px-Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg)

Menken as _The French Spy,_ 1863

After Cuba, Menken left dance for acting, and began working as an actress in Texas first. According to Gregory Eiselein, she gave [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") readings, and wrote poems and sketches for _The Liberty Gazette._ She was married for the first time in [Galveston County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston_County,_Texas "Galveston County, Texas"), in February 1855, to G. W. Kneass, a musician. The marriage had ended by sometime in 1856,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) when she met and in 1856 married the man more generally considered her first husband, Alexander Isaac Menken, a musician who was from a prominent [Reform Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Judaism "Reform Judaism") family in [Cincinnati, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

He began to act as her manager, and Ada Menken performed as an actress in the Midwest and Upper South, also giving literary readings. She received decent reviews, which noted her "reckless energy," and performed with men who became notable actors: [Edwin Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Booth "Edwin Booth") in [Louisville, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisville,_Kentucky "Louisville, Kentucky"), and James E. Murdoch in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12)

In 1857, the couple moved to [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati "Cincinnati"), where Menken created her Jewish roots, telling a reporter that she was born Jewish. She did study [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism") and stayed with the faith, although she never formally converted.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) In this period, she published poetry and articles on Judaism in _[The Israelite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Israelite "The Israelite")_ in Cincinnati.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12) The newspaper was founded by Rabbi [Isaac Mayer Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Mayer_Wise "Isaac Mayer Wise"), who was crucial to the [Reform Judaism movement in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Judaism#America_and_Classical_Reform "Reform Judaism").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Virt-13) She also began to be published in the _[Jewish Messenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish\_Messenger?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jewish Messenger (page does not exist)")_ of New York.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)

Ada added an "h" to her first name and an "s" to Isaac, and by 1858 she billed herself as Adah Isaacs Menken. She eventually worked as an actress in New York and San Francisco, as well as in touring productions across the country.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-14) She also became known for her poetry and painting. While none of her art was well received by major critics, she became a celebrity.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

At this time, Menken wore her wavy hair short, a highly unusual style for women of the time. She cultivated a [bohemian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemianism "Bohemianism") and at times [androgynous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgyny "Androgyny") appearance. She deliberately created her image at a time when the growth of popular media helped to publicize it.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

In 1859, Menken appeared on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") in New York City in the play _[The French Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_French\_Spy "The French Spy")._ Her work was not highly regarded by critics. _The New York Times_ described her as "the worst actress on Broadway." _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] said, "she is delightfully unhampered by the shackles of talent." Menken continued to perform small parts in New York, as well as reading Shakespeare in performance, and giving lectures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4)

Her third husband was [John C. Heenan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Heenan "John C. Heenan"), a popular Irish-American [prizefighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") whom she married in 1859. Some time after their marriage, the press discovered she did not yet have a legal divorce from Menken and accused her of [bigamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigamy "Bigamy"). She had expected Menken to handle the divorce, which he eventually did.

As John Heenan was one of the most famous and popular figures in America, the press also accused Menken of marrying for his celebrity. She billed herself as Mrs. Heenan in Boston, Providence, Baltimore, and Philadelphia, using his name despite their divorce within a year of marriage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) They had a son, who died soon after birth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

While in New York, Menken met the poet [Walt Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Whitman "Walt Whitman") and some others of his bohemian circle. She was influenced by his work and began to write in a more confessional style while adhering to common sentimental conventions of the time. In 1860–61, she published 25 poems in the _[Sunday Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Mercury\_(New\_York) "Sunday Mercury (New York)"),_ an entertainment newspaper in New York. These were later collected with six more in her only book, _[Infelicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infelicia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Infelicia (page does not exist)"),_ published a few months after her death.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12) By publishing in a newspaper, she reached a larger audience than through women's magazines, including both men and women readers who might go to see her perform as an actress.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

In 1860, Menken wrote a review titled "Swimming Against the Current," which praised Whitman's new edition of _[Leaves of Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves\_of\_Grass "Leaves of Grass"),_ saying he was "centuries ahead of his contemporaries."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Alcaro-15) She identified with the controversial poet, and declared her bohemian identity through her support for him.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) That year, Menken also wrote an article on the [1860 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_election "1860 election"), an unusual topic for a woman, which further added to her image.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

When Menken met [Charles Blondin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Blondin "Charles Blondin"), notable for crossing [Niagara Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls "Niagara Falls") on a tightrope, the two were quickly attracted to each other. She suggested she would marry him if they could perform a couple's act above the falls. Blondin refused, saying that he would be "distracted by her beauty."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) The two had an affair, during which they conducted a [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") tour across the United States.

## _Mazeppa_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mazeppa")]

See also: [Cultural legacy of Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_legacy_of_Mazeppa "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken%2C_Mazeppa%2C_TCS_19.jpg/250px-Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken%2C_Mazeppa%2C_TCS_19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken,_Mazeppa,_TCS_19.jpg)

Menken in _Mazeppa_, 1866

After it ended, she appealed to her business manager Jimmie Murdock to help her become recognized as a great actress. Murdock dissuaded Menken from that goal, as he believed she had little acting talent.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) He offered her the "[breeches role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breeches_role "Breeches role")" (that of a man) of the noble [Tartar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars") in the [hippodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippodrama "Hippodrama")_[Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural\_legacy\_of\_Mazeppa#The\_1830s-1860s "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa"),_ based on [the poem of that title by Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazeppa_(poem) "Mazeppa (poem)")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) (and ultimately on the life of [Ivan Mazepa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Mazepa "Ivan Mazepa")). At the climax of this hit, the Tartar was stripped of his clothing, tied to his horse, and sent off to his death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Buszek-16) The audiences were thrilled with the scene, although the production used a dummy strapped to a horse, which was led away by a handler giving sugar cubes. Menken wanted to perform the stunt herself.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) Dressed in nude tights and riding a horse on stage, she appeared to be naked and caused a sensation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) New York audiences were shocked but still attended and made the play popular.

Menken took the production of _Mazeppa_ to San Francisco, where it continued to be well-attended.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-17) She became known across the country for this role, and San Francisco adopted her as its performer.

In 1862, she married [Robert Henry Newell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Henry_Newell "Robert Henry Newell"), a humorist and editor of the _[Sunday Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Mercury\_(New\_York) "Sunday Mercury (New York)")_ in New York, who had recently published most of her poetry. They were together about three years. In 1866, she wed James Paul Barkley, a gambler, but soon returned without him to France, where she was performing. There she had their son, whom she named Louis Dudevant Victor Emanuel Barkley. The baby's godmother was the author [George Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Sand "George Sand") (A. F. Lesser).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) Louis died in infancy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley%27s_Amphitheatre%2C_1808_-_cropped.jpg/250px-Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley%27s_Amphitheatre%2C_1808_-_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley's_Amphitheatre,_1808_-_cropped.jpg)

A previous version of [Astley's Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astley's_Amphitheatre "Astley's Amphitheatre"), showing the horse ring

Menken arranged to play in a production of _Mazeppa_ in London and France for much of 1864 to 1866. Controversy arose over her costume, and she responded to critics in the newspapers of London by saying that she was influenced by classical sculpture, and that her costume was more modest than those of ballet or [burlesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlesque "Burlesque"). The show opened on October 3, 1864, at the [Astley Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astley's_Amphitheatre "Astley's Amphitheatre") to "overflowing houses."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Diamond-18) She was so well known that she was referred to as "the Menken," needing no other name.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

Jokes and poems were printed about the controversy, and _[Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch\_(magazine) "Punch (magazine)")_ wrote:[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Diamond-18)

> Here's half the town - if bills be true -  
>  To Astley's nightly thronging,  
>  To see the Menken throw aside  
>  All to her sex belonging,  
>  Stripping off woman's modesty,  
>  With woman's outward trappings -  
>  A barebacked jade on barebacked steed,  
>  In Cartlich's old strappings!

(The last line refers to John Cartlich, equestrian performer [[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-19))

At this lucrative height of her career, she was generous to friends, theatre workers in need, and charities.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) While in Europe, Menken's image continued to play to the American public as well.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) She attracted a crowd of male admirers, including writer [Charles Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens "Charles Dickens"), humorist [Tom Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hood "Tom Hood"), and dramatist and novelist [Charles Reade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reade "Charles Reade").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Schuele-20)

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later life")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Alexandre_Dumas_%26_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg/250px-Alexandre_Dumas_%26_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexandre_Dumas_&_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg)

Menken with Alexandre Dumas, 1866

Playing in a sold-out run of _Les pirates de la savane_ in Paris in 1866, Menken had an affair with the French novelist [Alexandre Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Dumas "Alexandre Dumas"), père, considered somewhat scandalous as he was more than twice her age. Returning to England in 1867, she struggled to attract audiences to _Mazeppa_ and attendance fell off. During this time she had an affair with the English poet [Algernon Charles Swinburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Charles_Swinburne "Algernon Charles Swinburne").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1)

She fell ill in London and was forced to stop performing, struggling with poverty as a result. Few realized that the glamorous star was ill until she collapsed during rehearsal and died a few weeks later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4) She began preparing her poems for publication and moved back to Paris, where she died on August 10, 1868, around the age of 33.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) Shortly before her death, she wrote to a friend:

> I am lost to art and life. Yet, when all is said and done, have I not at my age tasted more of life than most women who live to be a hundred? It is fair, then, that I should go where old people go.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

Menken was believed to have died of [peritonitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peritonitis "Peritonitis") and/or [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) Late twentieth-century sources suggest she had [cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) She was buried in [Montparnasse Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montparnasse_Cemetery "Montparnasse Cemetery"), a Jewish cemetery.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) The inscription on her tomb reads "Thou knowest," an epitaph she had chosen from Swinburne, the poet who had said of her, “A woman who has such beautiful legs need not discuss poetry.” [[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-21)

In 1862, Menken had written about her public and private personae:

> I have always believed myself to be possessed of two souls, one that lives on the surface of life, pleasing and pleased; the other as deep and as unfathomable as the ocean; a mystery to me and all who know me.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Notes-5)

Her only book, _Infelicia_, a collection of 31 poems, was published several days after her death.

## Literary career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Literary career")]

Menken wanted to be known as a writer, but her work was overshadowed by her sensational stage career and private and public life. In total, she published about 20 essays, 100 poems and a book of her collected poems, from 1855 to 1868; the book was published posthumously. Her work was not received well by contemporary critics. George Merriam Hyde, one of the most respected critics of his day, refused to critique Menken's work, saying privately that "it would be an insult to himself and his profession".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][Van Wyck Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Wyck_Brooks "Van Wyck Brooks") publicly joked that "her work is the best example of unintentional wit and accidental humour".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Her early work was devoted to family and romance. After her marriage to Menken and her study of Judaism, her poetry and essays for years into the 1860s featured Jewish themes. After her marriage and divorce from Heenan and meeting with writers in New York, she changed her style, adopting some influence from [Walt Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Whitman "Walt Whitman"). She was said to be the "first poet and the only woman poet before the twentieth century" to follow his lead in using free verse.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)_The New York Times_ reported that Walt Whitman had disassociated himself from Menken's work, implying he thought little of it.

Beginning in New York, her poetry expressed a wider range of emotions related to relationships, sexuality, and also about women's struggle to find a place in the world. Her collection _Infelicia_ went through several editions and was in print until 1902. In the late nineteenth century, critics were hard on women writers, and Menken's public notoriety caused even more critical scrutiny of her poems. Later critics (such as A. R. Lloyd in his book, _The Great Prize Fight_ and Graham Gordon in his book _Master of the Ring_) generally dismiss her work as being devoid of talent. Admirers included [Christina Rossetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Rossetti "Christina Rossetti") and [Joaquin Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaquin_Miller "Joaquin Miller").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)

American actress, dancer, painter, and poet (1835–1868)

**Adah Isaacs Menken** (June 15, 1835–August 10, 1868) was an American actress, painter and poet, and was the highest earning actress of her time.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) She was best known for her performance in the [hippodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippodrama "Hippodrama")_[Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural\_legacy\_of\_Mazeppa#The\_1830s-1860s "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa")_, with a climax that featured her apparently nude and riding a horse on stage. After great success for a few years with the play in New York and San Francisco, she appeared in a production in London and Paris, from 1864 to 1866. After a brief trip back to the United States, she returned to Europe. She became ill within two years and died in Paris at the age of 33.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-2)

Menken told many versions of her origins, including her name, place of birth, ancestry, and religion, and historians have differed in their accounts. Most have said she was born a [Louisiana Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people") Catholic, with European and African ancestry. A celebrity who created sensational performances in the United States and Europe, she married several times and was also known for her affairs. She had two sons, both of whom died in infancy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-3)

Though she was better known as an actress, Menken sought to be known as a writer. She published about 20 essays, 100 poems, and a book of her collected poems, from 1855 to 1868 (the book was published posthumously). Early work was devoted to family and after her marriage, her poetry and essays featured Jewish themes. Beginning with work published after moving to New York, with which she changed her style, Menken expressed a wide range of emotions and ideas about women's place in the world. Her collection _Infelicia_ went through several editions and was in print until 1902.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Accounts of Menken's early life and origins vary considerably. In her autobiographical "Some Notes of Her Life in Her Own Hand," published in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ in 1868, Menken said she was born in [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux "Bordeaux"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), and lived in [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba") as a child before her family settled in [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"). There are many conflicting reports as to Menken's birth name, but she has been called Marie Rachel Adelaide de Vere Spenser and Adah Bertha Theodore, and Ed James, a journalist friend, wrote after her death: "Her real name was Adelaide McCord, and she was born at [Milneburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milneburg "Milneburg"), near New Orleans, on June 15, 1835."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4) Menken's birth year also varies, with some records stating 1835 and some stating 1832.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Notes-5) Elsewhere, in 1865, she wrote that her birth name was Dolores Adios Los Fiertes, and that she was the daughter of a French woman from New Orleans and a [Spanish-Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Jews "Spanish Jews") man.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) About 1940, the consensus of scholars was that her parents were Auguste Théodore, a [free Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_black "Free black") man, and Marie, a [mixed-race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-race "Mixed-race") Creole, and Adah was raised as a Catholic. She had a sister and a brother.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)

Based on Menken's assertions of being a native of New Orleans, [Wolf Mankowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf_Mankowitz "Wolf Mankowitz") and others have studied Board of Health records for the city. They have concluded that Ada was born in the city as the legitimate daughter of Auguste Théodore, a [free man of color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_people_of_color "Free people of color") (mixed race) and his wife Magdaleine Jean Louis Janneaux,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-7) likely also a [Louisiana Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people"). Ada would have been raised as Catholic. However, in 1990, John Cofran, using census records, said that she was born as Ada C. McCord, in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), in late 1830. He said she was the daughter of an Irish merchant, Richard McCord, and his wife Catherine.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) According to Cofran, her father died when she was young and her mother remarried. The family then moved from Memphis to New Orleans.

Menken was said to have been a bright student; she became fluent in French and Spanish,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) and was described as having a gift for languages.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) As a child, Menken performed as a dancer in the ballet of the [French Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Opera_House "French Opera House") in New Orleans. In her later childhood, she performed as a dancer in [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"), [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"), where she was crowned "Queen of the Plaza."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

## American career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: American career")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg/250px-Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg)

Menken as _The French Spy,_ 1863

After Cuba, Menken left dance for acting, and began working as an actress in Texas first. According to Gregory Eiselein, she gave [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare") readings, and wrote poems and sketches for _The Liberty Gazette._ She was married for the first time in [Galveston County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galveston_County,_Texas "Galveston County, Texas"), in February 1855, to G. W. Kneass, a musician. The marriage had ended by sometime in 1856,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) when she met and in 1856 married the man more generally considered her first husband, Alexander Isaac Menken, a musician who was from a prominent [Reform Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Judaism "Reform Judaism") family in [Cincinnati, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

He began to act as her manager, and Ada Menken performed as an actress in the Midwest and Upper South, also giving literary readings. She received decent reviews, which noted her "reckless energy," and performed with men who became notable actors: [Edwin Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Booth "Edwin Booth") in [Louisville, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisville,_Kentucky "Louisville, Kentucky"), and James E. Murdoch in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12)

In 1857, the couple moved to [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati "Cincinnati"), where Menken created her Jewish roots, telling a reporter that she was born Jewish. She did study [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism") and stayed with the faith, although she never formally converted.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6) In this period, she published poetry and articles on Judaism in _[The Israelite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Israelite "The Israelite")_ in Cincinnati.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12) The newspaper was founded by Rabbi [Isaac Mayer Wise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Mayer_Wise "Isaac Mayer Wise"), who was crucial to the [Reform Judaism movement in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Judaism#America_and_Classical_Reform "Reform Judaism").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Virt-13) She also began to be published in the _[Jewish Messenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish\_Messenger?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jewish Messenger (page does not exist)")_ of New York.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)

Ada added an "h" to her first name and an "s" to Isaac, and by 1858 she billed herself as Adah Isaacs Menken. She eventually worked as an actress in New York and San Francisco, as well as in touring productions across the country.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-14) She also became known for her poetry and painting. While none of her art was well received by major critics, she became a celebrity.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

At this time, Menken wore her wavy hair short, a highly unusual style for women of the time. She cultivated a [bohemian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemianism "Bohemianism") and at times [androgynous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Androgyny "Androgyny") appearance. She deliberately created her image at a time when the growth of popular media helped to publicize it.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

In 1859, Menken appeared on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") in New York City in the play _[The French Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_French\_Spy "The French Spy")._ Her work was not highly regarded by critics. _The New York Times_ described her as "the worst actress on Broadway." _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] said, "she is delightfully unhampered by the shackles of talent." Menken continued to perform small parts in New York, as well as reading Shakespeare in performance, and giving lectures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4)

Her third husband was [John C. Heenan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Heenan "John C. Heenan"), a popular Irish-American [prizefighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") whom she married in 1859. Some time after their marriage, the press discovered she did not yet have a legal divorce from Menken and accused her of [bigamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigamy "Bigamy"). She had expected Menken to handle the divorce, which he eventually did.

As John Heenan was one of the most famous and popular figures in America, the press also accused Menken of marrying for his celebrity. She billed herself as Mrs. Heenan in Boston, Providence, Baltimore, and Philadelphia, using his name despite their divorce within a year of marriage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) They had a son, who died soon after birth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

While in New York, Menken met the poet [Walt Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Whitman "Walt Whitman") and some others of his bohemian circle. She was influenced by his work and began to write in a more confessional style while adhering to common sentimental conventions of the time. In 1860–61, she published 25 poems in the _[Sunday Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Mercury\_(New\_York) "Sunday Mercury (New York)"),_ an entertainment newspaper in New York. These were later collected with six more in her only book, _[Infelicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infelicia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Infelicia (page does not exist)"),_ published a few months after her death.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12) By publishing in a newspaper, she reached a larger audience than through women's magazines, including both men and women readers who might go to see her perform as an actress.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

In 1860, Menken wrote a review titled "Swimming Against the Current," which praised Whitman's new edition of _[Leaves of Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves\_of\_Grass "Leaves of Grass"),_ saying he was "centuries ahead of his contemporaries."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Haralson-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Alcaro-15) She identified with the controversial poet, and declared her bohemian identity through her support for him.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) That year, Menken also wrote an article on the [1860 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_election "1860 election"), an unusual topic for a woman, which further added to her image.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

When Menken met [Charles Blondin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Blondin "Charles Blondin"), notable for crossing [Niagara Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls "Niagara Falls") on a tightrope, the two were quickly attracted to each other. She suggested she would marry him if they could perform a couple's act above the falls. Blondin refused, saying that he would be "distracted by her beauty."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) The two had an affair, during which they conducted a [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") tour across the United States.

## _Mazeppa_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mazeppa")]

See also: [Cultural legacy of Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_legacy_of_Mazeppa "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken%2C_Mazeppa%2C_TCS_19.jpg/250px-Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken%2C_Mazeppa%2C_TCS_19.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harvard_Theatre_Collection_-_Menken,_Mazeppa,_TCS_19.jpg)

Menken in _Mazeppa_, 1866

After it ended, she appealed to her business manager Jimmie Murdock to help her become recognized as a great actress. Murdock dissuaded Menken from that goal, as he believed she had little acting talent.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) He offered her the "[breeches role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breeches_role "Breeches role")" (that of a man) of the noble [Tartar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars") in the [hippodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippodrama "Hippodrama")_[Mazeppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural\_legacy\_of\_Mazeppa#The\_1830s-1860s "Cultural legacy of Mazeppa"),_ based on [the poem of that title by Lord Byron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazeppa_(poem) "Mazeppa (poem)")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) (and ultimately on the life of [Ivan Mazepa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Mazepa "Ivan Mazepa")). At the climax of this hit, the Tartar was stripped of his clothing, tied to his horse, and sent off to his death.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Buszek-16) The audiences were thrilled with the scene, although the production used a dummy strapped to a horse, which was led away by a handler giving sugar cubes. Menken wanted to perform the stunt herself.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) Dressed in nude tights and riding a horse on stage, she appeared to be naked and caused a sensation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Brooks-9) New York audiences were shocked but still attended and made the play popular.

Menken took the production of _Mazeppa_ to San Francisco, where it continued to be well-attended.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-17) She became known across the country for this role, and San Francisco adopted her as its performer.

In 1862, she married [Robert Henry Newell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Henry_Newell "Robert Henry Newell"), a humorist and editor of the _[Sunday Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Mercury\_(New\_York) "Sunday Mercury (New York)")_ in New York, who had recently published most of her poetry. They were together about three years. In 1866, she wed James Paul Barkley, a gambler, but soon returned without him to France, where she was performing. There she had their son, whom she named Louis Dudevant Victor Emanuel Barkley. The baby's godmother was the author [George Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Sand "George Sand") (A. F. Lesser).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) Louis died in infancy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley%27s_Amphitheatre%2C_1808_-_cropped.jpg/250px-Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley%27s_Amphitheatre%2C_1808_-_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Houghton_57-1633_-_Astley's_Amphitheatre,_1808_-_cropped.jpg)

A previous version of [Astley's Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astley's_Amphitheatre "Astley's Amphitheatre"), showing the horse ring

Menken arranged to play in a production of _Mazeppa_ in London and France for much of 1864 to 1866. Controversy arose over her costume, and she responded to critics in the newspapers of London by saying that she was influenced by classical sculpture, and that her costume was more modest than those of ballet or [burlesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlesque "Burlesque"). The show opened on October 3, 1864, at the [Astley Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astley's_Amphitheatre "Astley's Amphitheatre") to "overflowing houses."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Diamond-18) She was so well known that she was referred to as "the Menken," needing no other name.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11)

Jokes and poems were printed about the controversy, and _[Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch\_(magazine) "Punch (magazine)")_ wrote:[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Diamond-18)

> Here's half the town - if bills be true -  
>  To Astley's nightly thronging,  
>  To see the Menken throw aside  
>  All to her sex belonging,  
>  Stripping off woman's modesty,  
>  With woman's outward trappings -  
>  A barebacked jade on barebacked steed,  
>  In Cartlich's old strappings!

(The last line refers to John Cartlich, equestrian performer [[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-19))

At this lucrative height of her career, she was generous to friends, theatre workers in need, and charities.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) While in Europe, Menken's image continued to play to the American public as well.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-menken1-11) She attracted a crowd of male admirers, including writer [Charles Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens "Charles Dickens"), humorist [Tom Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hood "Tom Hood"), and dramatist and novelist [Charles Reade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Reade "Charles Reade").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Schuele-20)

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Later life")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Alexandre_Dumas_%26_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg/250px-Alexandre_Dumas_%26_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexandre_Dumas_&_Adah_Isaacs_Menken.jpg)

Menken with Alexandre Dumas, 1866

Playing in a sold-out run of _Les pirates de la savane_ in Paris in 1866, Menken had an affair with the French novelist [Alexandre Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Dumas "Alexandre Dumas"), père, considered somewhat scandalous as he was more than twice her age. Returning to England in 1867, she struggled to attract audiences to _Mazeppa_ and attendance fell off. During this time she had an affair with the English poet [Algernon Charles Swinburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Charles_Swinburne "Algernon Charles Swinburne").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1)

She fell ill in London and was forced to stop performing, struggling with poverty as a result. Few realized that the glamorous star was ill until she collapsed during rehearsal and died a few weeks later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Barca-4) She began preparing her poems for publication and moved back to Paris, where she died on August 10, 1868, around the age of 33.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) Shortly before her death, she wrote to a friend:

> I am lost to art and life. Yet, when all is said and done, have I not at my age tasted more of life than most women who live to be a hundred? It is fair, then, that I should go where old people go.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10)

Menken was believed to have died of [peritonitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peritonitis "Peritonitis") and/or [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-SanFran-10) Late twentieth-century sources suggest she had [cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) She was buried in [Montparnasse Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montparnasse_Cemetery "Montparnasse Cemetery"), a Jewish cemetery.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Palmer-1) The inscription on her tomb reads "Thou knowest," an epitaph she had chosen from Swinburne, the poet who had said of her, “A woman who has such beautiful legs need not discuss poetry.” [[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-21)

In 1862, Menken had written about her public and private personae:

> I have always believed myself to be possessed of two souls, one that lives on the surface of life, pleasing and pleased; the other as deep and as unfathomable as the ocean; a mystery to me and all who know me.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Notes-5)

Her only book, _Infelicia_, a collection of 31 poems, was published several days after her death.

## Literary career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adah_Isaacs_Menken&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Literary career")]

Menken wanted to be known as a writer, but her work was overshadowed by her sensational stage career and private and public life. In total, she published about 20 essays, 100 poems and a book of her collected poems, from 1855 to 1868; the book was published posthumously. Her work was not received well by contemporary critics. George Merriam Hyde, one of the most respected critics of his day, refused to critique Menken's work, saying privately that "it would be an insult to himself and his profession".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][Van Wyck Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Wyck_Brooks "Van Wyck Brooks") publicly joked that "her work is the best example of unintentional wit and accidental humour".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Her early work was devoted to family and romance. After her marriage to Menken and her study of Judaism, her poetry and essays for years into the 1860s featured Jewish themes. After her marriage and divorce from Heenan and meeting with writers in New York, she changed her style, adopting some influence from [Walt Whitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Whitman "Walt Whitman"). She was said to be the "first poet and the only woman poet before the twentieth century" to follow his lead in using free verse.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)_The New York Times_ reported that Walt Whitman had disassociated himself from Menken's work, implying he thought little of it.

Beginning in New York, her poetry expressed a wider range of emotions related to relationships, sexuality, and also about women's struggle to find a place in the world. Her collection _Infelicia_ went through several editions and was in print until 1902. In the late nineteenth century, critics were hard on women writers, and Menken's public notoriety caused even more critical scrutiny of her poems. Later critics (such as A. R. Lloyd in his book, _The Great Prize Fight_ and Graham Gordon in his book _Master of the Ring_) generally dismiss her work as being devoid of talent. Admirers included [Christina Rossetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Rossetti "Christina Rossetti") and [Joaquin Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaquin_Miller "Joaquin Miller").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adah_Isaacs_Menken#cite_note-Eiselein-6)
