_**The Nation**_ is a [left-leaning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-leaning "Left-leaning")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-2) and [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism") American monthly magazine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3) It covers politics and culture and bills itself as "the flagship of the left".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:2-4)_The Nation_ was once the oldest weekly magazine in the US, but is now published on a monthly basis.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-6) It publishes articles by various high-profile American academics and activists. _[Jacobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobin\_(magazine) "Jacobin (magazine)")_ founder [Bhaskar Sunkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaskar_Sunkara "Bhaskar Sunkara") is the president of the magazine.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:5-7)

It was founded on July 6, 1865, as a successor to [William Lloyd Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lloyd_Garrison "William Lloyd Garrison")'s _[The Liberator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Liberator\_(newspaper) "The Liberator (newspaper)")_, an [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States") newspaper that closed in 1865, after ratification of the [Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution"). Thereafter, the magazine proceeded to a broader topic, _The Nation_. An important collaborator of the new magazine was its Literary Editor [Wendell Phillips Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendell_Phillips_Garrison "Wendell Phillips Garrison"), son of William. He had at his disposal his father's vast network of contacts.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:6-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:7-9)

_The Nation_ is published by its namesake owner, The Nation Company, L.P., at 520 8th Ave New York, NY 10018. It has news bureaus in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), and [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), with departments covering [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture"), art, corporations, [defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military "Military"), [environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment"), films, [legal affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), music, [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace") and [disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disarmament "Disarmament"), poetry, and the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"). Circulation peaked at 187,000 in 2006 but dropped to 145,000 in print by 2010, although digital subscriptions had risen to over 15,000. By 2021, the total for both print and digital combined was 96,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Media_Kit-10)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding and journalistic roots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding and journalistic roots")]

_The Nation_ was established on July 6, 1865, at 130 Nassau Street ("[Newspaper Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Row_(Manhattan) "Park Row (Manhattan)")") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). Its founding coincided with the closure of the abolitionist newspaper _[The Liberator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Liberator\_(newspaper) "The Liberator (newspaper)")_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:7-9) also in 1865, after slavery was abolished by the [Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution"); a group of abolitionists, led by the landscape architect [Frederick Law Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Law_Olmsted "Frederick Law Olmsted"), desired to found a new weekly political magazine. [Edwin Lawrence Godkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Lawrence_Godkin "Edwin Lawrence Godkin"), who had been considering starting such a magazine for some time, agreed and so became the first editor of _The Nation_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:6-8)

Its founding publisher was Joseph H. Richards; the editor was Godkin, an [immigrant from Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_American "Irish American") who had formerly worked as a correspondent of the London _[Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_News\_(UK) "The Daily News (UK)")_ and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-ja-12) Godkin sought to establish what one sympathetic commentator later characterized as "an organ of opinion characterized in its utterance by breadth and deliberation, an organ which should identify itself with causes, and which should give its support to parties primarily as representative of these causes".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503

In its "founding prospectus" the magazine wrote that the publication would have "seven main objects" with the first being "discussion of the topics of the day, and, above all, of legal, economical, and constitutional questions, with greater accuracy and moderation than are now to be found in the daily press". _The Nation_ pledged to "not be the organ of any party, sect or body" but rather to "make an earnest effort to bring to discussion of political and social questions a really critical spirit, and to wage war upon the vices of violence, exaggeration and misrepresentation by which so much of the political writing of the day is marred".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-FoundingProspectus-13)

In the first year of publication, one of the magazine's regular features was _The South as It Is._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-14) The magazine published eyewitness accounts of the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era") of southern states.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:3-15)

Among the causes supported by the publication in its earliest days was civil service reform—moving the basis of government employment from a [political patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_patronage "Political patronage") system to a professional [bureaucracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureaucracy "Bureaucracy") based upon [meritocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meritocracy "Meritocracy").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503 _The Nation_ also was preoccupied with the reestablishment of a sound national currency in the years after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), arguing that a stable [currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency "Currency") was necessary to restore the economic stability of the nation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503–504 Closely related to this was the publication's advocacy of the elimination of [protective tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protective_tariffs "Protective tariffs") in favor of lower prices of consumer goods associated with a [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade") system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):504

### From 1880s literary supplement to 1930s New Deal booster

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: From 1880s literary supplement to 1930s New Deal booster")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/%28King1893NYC%29_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION%2C_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-%28King1893NYC%29_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION%2C_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(King1893NYC)_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION,_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_(cropped).jpg)

_The Evening Post_ and _The Nation_, 210 Broadway, Manhattan, New York

In June 1881, _The Nation_ was acquired by journalist [Henry Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Villard "Henry Villard").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16) Afterwards, the magazine was printed in conjunction with _New York Evening Post_ _(_ now _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_), which at the time held [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States") views _._[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:4-17)

After Henry Villard died, the publications were inherited by his son; [Oswald Garrison Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_Garrison_Villard "Oswald Garrison Villard").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-18) Villard's ideology and the editorial stance of _The Nation_ shared many similarities; both were advocating for [racial equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_equality "Racial equality") and [isolationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolationism "Isolationism").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:4-17) In July 1918, Villard announced that _The Nation_ will be separate from the newspaper and stop reprinting articles of the _New York Evening Post_. Villard made this decision because he believed that reprinting practice gave readers the impression that _The Nation_ was a weekly publication of the _New York Evening Post_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-19)

As the 1932 U.S. presidential election approached, _The Nation_ saw no real choice between Hoover and Roosevelt, and it urged readers to vote for [Socialist Party of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_of_America "Socialist Party of America") candidate [Norman Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Thomas "Norman Thomas"). Oswald Villard wrote: "So I insist, the man who votes for either Hoover or Roosevelt is the one who is throwing away his vote... He is again postponing the peaceful revolution which Woodrow Wilson said in 1912 was on the horizon." The magazine did, however, endorse Roosevelt in the next three elections.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-20)

Oswald Villard welcomed the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal") and supported the [nationalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization "Nationalization") of industries—thus reversing the meaning of "[liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism")" as the founders of _The Nation_ would have understood the term, from a belief in a smaller and more restricted government to a belief in a larger and less restricted government.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-22) Villard sold the magazine in 1935 to "The Nation Fund, Inc", a [nonprofit corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_corporation "Nonprofit corporation") established by banker [Maurice Wertheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wertheim "Maurice Wertheim").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-23) In 1937, Wertheim sold _The Nation_ to editor [Freda Kirchwey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freda_Kirchwey "Freda Kirchwey"), who said she bought it because she intended to turn the magazine into a "voice of [leftism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leftism "Leftism")".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-24)

Almost every editor of _The Nation_ from Villard's time to the 1970s was looked at for "subversive" activities and ties.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-25) When [Albert Jay Nock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Jay_Nock "Albert Jay Nock") published a column criticizing [Samuel Gompers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Gompers "Samuel Gompers") and trade unions for being complicit in the war machine of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), _The Nation_ was briefly suspended from the US mail.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-26)

### World War II and early Cold War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War II and early Cold War")]

The magazine's financial problems in the early 1940s prompted Kirchwey to sell her individual ownership of the magazine in 1943, creating a [nonprofit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization") organization; Nation Associates, out of the money generated from a recruiting drive of sponsors. This organization was also responsible for academic affairs, including conducting research and organizing conferences, that had been a part of the early history of the magazine. Nation Associates became responsible for the operation and publication of the magazine on a nonprofit basis, with Kirchwey as both president of Nation Associates and editor of _The Nation_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-27)

Before the [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor"), _The Nation_ repeatedly called on the United States to enter World War II to resist [fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism"), and after the US entered the war, the publication supported the American war effort. Furthermore, unlike other leftist publications and organizations which followed a close Stalinist line in keeping with the [Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov-Ribbentrop_Pact "Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact"), _The Nation_ supported American intervention in the war before [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-pfb-28) It also supported the use of the [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") on [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-pfb-28)

In January 1942, [The Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust") committed by Nazi Germany received almost no attention from the global media. _The Nation_ was one of the few publications that reported on the crimes committed against Jews during this period; it published multiple articles by Rabbi [Philip S. Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sidney_Bernstein "Philip Sidney Bernstein"), who explained the events that took place in the [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camp "Concentration camp") run by the [Schutzstaffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutzstaffel "Schutzstaffel"). _The Nation_ advocated for the United States to provide refuge to German Jewry.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16)

Freda Kirchwey openly supported the idea of banning the [fascist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism") press, which earned her the enmity of [liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States"), including her long-time friend [Norman Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Thomas "Norman Thomas") who said: "In ten years or less it won't be the people you want to suppress now who will be suppressed and stay suppressed by your theory; it will be yourselves along with many others".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16)

In the 1950s, _The Nation_ was attacked by critics as "pro-communist" because of its advocacy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the [expansionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Empire "Soviet Empire")[Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") of [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin"), and its criticism of [McCarthyism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism "McCarthyism").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-ja-12) One of the magazine's writers, [Louis Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Fischer "Louis Fischer"), resigned from the magazine afterwards, claiming _The Nation_'s foreign coverage was too pro-Soviet.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-fk-29) Despite this, [Diana Trilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Trilling "Diana Trilling") pointed out that Kirchwey did allow anti-Soviet writers, such as herself, to contribute material critical of Russia to the magazine's arts section.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-30)

During McCarthyism (the Second Red Scare), _The Nation_ was banned from several school libraries in New York City and Newark,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-dc-31) and a [Bartlesville, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartlesville,_Oklahoma "Bartlesville, Oklahoma"), librarian, [Ruth Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Brown_(librarian) "Ruth Brown (librarian)"), was fired from her job in 1950, after a citizens committee complained she had given shelf space to _The Nation_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-dc-31) In 1957, [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro") wrote an article for _The Nation_, titled; "What Cuba's Rebels Want". A year later, the magazine published an article discussing the possibility of US invading Cuba; it predicted the [Bay of Pigs invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Pigs_Invasion "Bay of Pigs Invasion").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:3-15)

In 1950, _The Nation_ published a report describing the [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company") as "an obstacle of progress in Central America". The company's president, [Sam Zemurray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Zemurray "Sam Zemurray"), disputed the characterization, yet after retiring the following year he became a substantial benefactor of the magazine at a time when it had fallen on hard times.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-33) In 1955, [George Kirstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kirstein "George Kirstein") replaced Freda Kirchway as magazine owner.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-34)[James J. Storrow Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_J._Storrow_Jr. "James J. Storrow Jr.") bought the magazine from Kirstein in 1965.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-35)

### 1970s to 2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1970s to 2024")]

See also: [Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation_Magazine_v._United_States_Department_of_Defense "Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense")

On the eve of the 1968 U.S. presidential election the magazine argued that the choice between Nixon and Humphrey was such a bad one that voters should stay home.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-36) In June 1979, _The Nation_'s publisher [Hamilton Fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Fish_V "Hamilton Fish V") moved the magazine to 72 [Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Avenue "Fifth Avenue"), in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:2-4)_The Nation's_ current address is 33 Irving Place in New York.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-37)

In 1977, a group organized by [Hamilton Fish V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Fish_V "Hamilton Fish V") bought the magazine from the Storrow family.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-38) In 1985, the magazine was sold to for undiscosed amount to "The Nation Co", headed by millionaire Arthur Carter and two former owners of _The Nation_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:0-39)

In March 1991, _The Nation_ together with [Center for Constitutional Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Constitutional_Rights "Center for Constitutional Rights") sued [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") for allegedly violating First Amendment and Fifth Amendment for creating [press pools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_pool "Press pool") during [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War"). Judge [Leonard B. Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_B._Sand "Leonard B. Sand") ruled the case [moot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mootness "Mootness").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-40) In 1995, veteran editor [Victor Navasky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Navasky "Victor Navasky") and a group of investors that included [Paul Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Newman "Paul Newman") acquired the magazine. Navasky became the magazine's publisher and editorial director.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-41) In 1995, [Katrina vanden Heuvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katrina_vanden_Heuvel "Katrina vanden Heuvel") succeeded Navasky as editor of _The Nation._[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-42) In 2005, she became the magazine's editor and publisher.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-43)

> "In an era of instant, 140-character news cycles and reflexive toeing of the party line, it's incredible to think of the 150-year history of The Nation. It's more than a magazine - it's a crucible of ideas forged in the time of Emancipation, tempered through depression and war and the civil-rights movement, and honed as sharp and relevant as ever in an age of breathtaking technological and economic change."

—[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"),per _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:obama-44)

In 2015, _The Nation_ celebrated its 150th anniversary with a documentary film by Academy Award–winning director [Barbara Kopple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Kopple "Barbara Kopple"), which analyzed the magazine's history.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-45)_The Nation_ also held a celebration in [St. Ann's Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Ann's_Warehouse "St. Ann's Warehouse") in Brooklyn, which was attended by [Tony Kushner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Kushner "Tony Kushner"), [Bill de Blasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_de_Blasio "Bill de Blasio"), [Walter Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mosley "Walter Mosley") and [Michael Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moore "Michael Moore").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-46) To mark the anniversary, former US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") wrote a letter praising _The Nation_ but noting that he disagreed with some of the magazine's views.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:obama-44) Editor of _The Nation_, [D. D. Guttenplan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._D._Guttenplan "D. D. Guttenplan") wrote a biography of the magazine entitled _The Nation: A Biography (The First 150 Years)_. [History News Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_News_Network "History News Network") said that the biography "has played, and continues to play, an important role in U.S. history, society, and politics".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-47)

In January 2016, _The Nation_ endorsed [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont")[Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") for [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") for the third time in its history. The editorial board professed; "Voters can trust Sanders because he doesn't owe his political career to the financial overlords of the status quo. Freed from these chains of special interest, he can take the bold measures that the country needs".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-48) On June 15, 2019, Heuvel stepped down as editor; D. D. Guttenplan, the editor-at-large, took her place.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-june2019-49)

On February 23, 2022, _The Nation_ named _[Jacobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobin\_(magazine) "Jacobin (magazine)")_ founder [Bhaskar Sunkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaskar_Sunkara "Bhaskar Sunkara") its new president. In an interview, Sunkara said that he believes [liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States") and [socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism "Socialism") need to form a coalition to ensure progress and him becoming a president of _The Nation_ was one way towards this goal.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:5-7) In December 2023, Sunkara announced the magazine would be switching from a biweekly format to a larger monthly publication.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3)

## Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Finances")]

Print ad pages declined by 5% from 2009 to 2010, while [digital advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_advertising "Digital advertising") rose 32.8% from 2009 to 2010.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-50) Advertising accounts for 10% of total revenue for the magazine, while circulation totals 60%.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-NYT1-51)_The Nation_ has lost money in all but three or four years of operation and is sustained in part by a group of more than 30,000 donors called Nation Associates, who donate funds to the periodical above and beyond their annual subscription fees. This program accounts for 30% of the total revenue for the magazine. An annual cruise also generates $200,000 for the magazine.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-NYT1-51) Since late 2012, the Nation Associates program has been called Nation Builders.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-52)

In 2023, the magazine had approximately 91,000 subscribers, roughly 80% of whom pay for the print magazine. Adding sales from newsstands, _The Nation_ had a total circulation of 96,000 copies per issue in 2021, earning the majority of its revenue from subscriptions and donations, rather than print advertising.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3)

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Poetry")]

Since its creation, _The Nation_ has published significant works of [American poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_poetry "American poetry"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54) including works by [Hart Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart_Crane "Hart Crane"), [Eli Siegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Siegel "Eli Siegel"), [Elizabeth Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bishop "Elizabeth Bishop"), and [Adrienne Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Rich "Adrienne Rich"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53) as well as [W. S. Merwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._S._Merwin "W. S. Merwin"), [Pablo Neruda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Neruda "Pablo Neruda"), [Denise Levertov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_Levertov "Denise Levertov"), and [Derek Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Walcott "Derek Walcott").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54)

In 2018, the magazine published a poem entitled "How-To" by Anders Carlson-Wee which was written in the voice of a homeless man and used [black vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Vernacular_English "African-American Vernacular English"). This led to criticism from writers such as [Roxane Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxane_Gay "Roxane Gay") because Carlson-Wee is white. _The Nation_'s two poetry editors, [Stephanie Burt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Burt "Stephanie Burt") and [Carmen Giménez Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Gim%C3%A9nez_Smith "Carmen Giménez Smith"), issued an apology for publishing the poem, the first such action ever taken by the magazine.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53) The apology itself became an object of criticism also. Poet and _Nation_ columnist [Katha Pollitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katha_Pollitt "Katha Pollitt") called the apology "craven" and likened it to a letter written from "a reeducation camp".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53)[Grace Schulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Schulman "Grace Schulman"), _The Nation_'s poetry editor from 1971 to 2006, wrote that the apology represented a disturbing departure from the magazine's traditionally broad conception of [artistic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_freedom "Artistic freedom").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54)

American monthly political magazine

For other uses, see [The Nation (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(disambiguation) "The Nation (disambiguation)").

_**The Nation**_ is a [left-leaning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-leaning "Left-leaning")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-2) and [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism "Progressivism") American monthly magazine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3) It covers politics and culture and bills itself as "the flagship of the left".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:2-4)_The Nation_ was once the oldest weekly magazine in the US, but is now published on a monthly basis.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-6) It publishes articles by various high-profile American academics and activists. _[Jacobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobin\_(magazine) "Jacobin (magazine)")_ founder [Bhaskar Sunkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaskar_Sunkara "Bhaskar Sunkara") is the president of the magazine.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:5-7)

It was founded on July 6, 1865, as a successor to [William Lloyd Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Lloyd_Garrison "William Lloyd Garrison")'s _[The Liberator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Liberator\_(newspaper) "The Liberator (newspaper)")_, an [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States") newspaper that closed in 1865, after ratification of the [Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution"). Thereafter, the magazine proceeded to a broader topic, _The Nation_. An important collaborator of the new magazine was its Literary Editor [Wendell Phillips Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendell_Phillips_Garrison "Wendell Phillips Garrison"), son of William. He had at his disposal his father's vast network of contacts.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:6-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:7-9)

_The Nation_ is published by its namesake owner, The Nation Company, L.P., at 520 8th Ave New York, NY 10018. It has news bureaus in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), and [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), with departments covering [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture"), art, corporations, [defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military "Military"), [environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_environment "Natural environment"), films, [legal affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), music, [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace") and [disarmament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disarmament "Disarmament"), poetry, and the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"). Circulation peaked at 187,000 in 2006 but dropped to 145,000 in print by 2010, although digital subscriptions had risen to over 15,000. By 2021, the total for both print and digital combined was 96,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Media_Kit-10)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding and journalistic roots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding and journalistic roots")]

_The Nation_ was established on July 6, 1865, at 130 Nassau Street ("[Newspaper Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Row_(Manhattan) "Park Row (Manhattan)")") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). Its founding coincided with the closure of the abolitionist newspaper _[The Liberator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Liberator\_(newspaper) "The Liberator (newspaper)")_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:7-9) also in 1865, after slavery was abolished by the [Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution"); a group of abolitionists, led by the landscape architect [Frederick Law Olmsted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Law_Olmsted "Frederick Law Olmsted"), desired to found a new weekly political magazine. [Edwin Lawrence Godkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Lawrence_Godkin "Edwin Lawrence Godkin"), who had been considering starting such a magazine for some time, agreed and so became the first editor of _The Nation_.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:6-8)

Its founding publisher was Joseph H. Richards; the editor was Godkin, an [immigrant from Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_American "Irish American") who had formerly worked as a correspondent of the London _[Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_News\_(UK) "The Daily News (UK)")_ and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-ja-12) Godkin sought to establish what one sympathetic commentator later characterized as "an organ of opinion characterized in its utterance by breadth and deliberation, an organ which should identify itself with causes, and which should give its support to parties primarily as representative of these causes".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503

In its "founding prospectus" the magazine wrote that the publication would have "seven main objects" with the first being "discussion of the topics of the day, and, above all, of legal, economical, and constitutional questions, with greater accuracy and moderation than are now to be found in the daily press". _The Nation_ pledged to "not be the organ of any party, sect or body" but rather to "make an earnest effort to bring to discussion of political and social questions a really critical spirit, and to wage war upon the vices of violence, exaggeration and misrepresentation by which so much of the political writing of the day is marred".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-FoundingProspectus-13)

In the first year of publication, one of the magazine's regular features was _The South as It Is._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-14) The magazine published eyewitness accounts of the [Reconstruction era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era") of southern states.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:3-15)

Among the causes supported by the publication in its earliest days was civil service reform—moving the basis of government employment from a [political patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_patronage "Political patronage") system to a professional [bureaucracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureaucracy "Bureaucracy") based upon [meritocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meritocracy "Meritocracy").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503 _The Nation_ also was preoccupied with the reestablishment of a sound national currency in the years after the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), arguing that a stable [currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency "Currency") was necessary to restore the economic stability of the nation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):503–504 Closely related to this was the publication's advocacy of the elimination of [protective tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protective_tariffs "Protective tariffs") in favor of lower prices of consumer goods associated with a [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade") system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-nation1917-11):504

### From 1880s literary supplement to 1930s New Deal booster

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: From 1880s literary supplement to 1930s New Deal booster")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/%28King1893NYC%29_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION%2C_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-%28King1893NYC%29_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION%2C_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:(King1893NYC)_pg617_THE_EVENING_POST_AND_THE_NATION,_EVENING_POST_BUILDING_(cropped).jpg)

_The Evening Post_ and _The Nation_, 210 Broadway, Manhattan, New York

In June 1881, _The Nation_ was acquired by journalist [Henry Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Villard "Henry Villard").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16) Afterwards, the magazine was printed in conjunction with _New York Evening Post_ _(_ now _[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Post "New York Post")_), which at the time held [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States") views _._[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:4-17)

After Henry Villard died, the publications were inherited by his son; [Oswald Garrison Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_Garrison_Villard "Oswald Garrison Villard").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-18) Villard's ideology and the editorial stance of _The Nation_ shared many similarities; both were advocating for [racial equality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_equality "Racial equality") and [isolationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isolationism "Isolationism").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:4-17) In July 1918, Villard announced that _The Nation_ will be separate from the newspaper and stop reprinting articles of the _New York Evening Post_. Villard made this decision because he believed that reprinting practice gave readers the impression that _The Nation_ was a weekly publication of the _New York Evening Post_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-19)

As the 1932 U.S. presidential election approached, _The Nation_ saw no real choice between Hoover and Roosevelt, and it urged readers to vote for [Socialist Party of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Party_of_America "Socialist Party of America") candidate [Norman Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Thomas "Norman Thomas"). Oswald Villard wrote: "So I insist, the man who votes for either Hoover or Roosevelt is the one who is throwing away his vote... He is again postponing the peaceful revolution which Woodrow Wilson said in 1912 was on the horizon." The magazine did, however, endorse Roosevelt in the next three elections.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-20)

Oswald Villard welcomed the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal") and supported the [nationalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization "Nationalization") of industries—thus reversing the meaning of "[liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism")" as the founders of _The Nation_ would have understood the term, from a belief in a smaller and more restricted government to a belief in a larger and less restricted government.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-22) Villard sold the magazine in 1935 to "The Nation Fund, Inc", a [nonprofit corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_corporation "Nonprofit corporation") established by banker [Maurice Wertheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wertheim "Maurice Wertheim").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-23) In 1937, Wertheim sold _The Nation_ to editor [Freda Kirchwey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freda_Kirchwey "Freda Kirchwey"), who said she bought it because she intended to turn the magazine into a "voice of [leftism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leftism "Leftism")".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-24)

Almost every editor of _The Nation_ from Villard's time to the 1970s was looked at for "subversive" activities and ties.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-25) When [Albert Jay Nock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Jay_Nock "Albert Jay Nock") published a column criticizing [Samuel Gompers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Gompers "Samuel Gompers") and trade unions for being complicit in the war machine of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), _The Nation_ was briefly suspended from the US mail.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-26)

### World War II and early Cold War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: World War II and early Cold War")]

The magazine's financial problems in the early 1940s prompted Kirchwey to sell her individual ownership of the magazine in 1943, creating a [nonprofit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization") organization; Nation Associates, out of the money generated from a recruiting drive of sponsors. This organization was also responsible for academic affairs, including conducting research and organizing conferences, that had been a part of the early history of the magazine. Nation Associates became responsible for the operation and publication of the magazine on a nonprofit basis, with Kirchwey as both president of Nation Associates and editor of _The Nation_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-27)

Before the [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor"), _The Nation_ repeatedly called on the United States to enter World War II to resist [fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism"), and after the US entered the war, the publication supported the American war effort. Furthermore, unlike other leftist publications and organizations which followed a close Stalinist line in keeping with the [Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov-Ribbentrop_Pact "Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact"), _The Nation_ supported American intervention in the war before [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa "Operation Barbarossa").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-pfb-28) It also supported the use of the [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") on [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki "Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-pfb-28)

In January 1942, [The Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust") committed by Nazi Germany received almost no attention from the global media. _The Nation_ was one of the few publications that reported on the crimes committed against Jews during this period; it published multiple articles by Rabbi [Philip S. Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sidney_Bernstein "Philip Sidney Bernstein"), who explained the events that took place in the [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camp "Concentration camp") run by the [Schutzstaffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutzstaffel "Schutzstaffel"). _The Nation_ advocated for the United States to provide refuge to German Jewry.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16)

Freda Kirchwey openly supported the idea of banning the [fascist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism") press, which earned her the enmity of [liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States"), including her long-time friend [Norman Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Thomas "Norman Thomas") who said: "In ten years or less it won't be the people you want to suppress now who will be suppressed and stay suppressed by your theory; it will be yourselves along with many others".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:8-16)

In the 1950s, _The Nation_ was attacked by critics as "pro-communist" because of its advocacy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the [expansionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Empire "Soviet Empire")[Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") of [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin"), and its criticism of [McCarthyism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism "McCarthyism").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-ja-12) One of the magazine's writers, [Louis Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Fischer "Louis Fischer"), resigned from the magazine afterwards, claiming _The Nation_'s foreign coverage was too pro-Soviet.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-fk-29) Despite this, [Diana Trilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Trilling "Diana Trilling") pointed out that Kirchwey did allow anti-Soviet writers, such as herself, to contribute material critical of Russia to the magazine's arts section.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-30)

During McCarthyism (the Second Red Scare), _The Nation_ was banned from several school libraries in New York City and Newark,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-dc-31) and a [Bartlesville, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartlesville,_Oklahoma "Bartlesville, Oklahoma"), librarian, [Ruth Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Brown_(librarian) "Ruth Brown (librarian)"), was fired from her job in 1950, after a citizens committee complained she had given shelf space to _The Nation_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-dc-31) In 1957, [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro "Fidel Castro") wrote an article for _The Nation_, titled; "What Cuba's Rebels Want". A year later, the magazine published an article discussing the possibility of US invading Cuba; it predicted the [Bay of Pigs invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Pigs_Invasion "Bay of Pigs Invasion").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:3-15)

In 1950, _The Nation_ published a report describing the [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company") as "an obstacle of progress in Central America". The company's president, [Sam Zemurray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Zemurray "Sam Zemurray"), disputed the characterization, yet after retiring the following year he became a substantial benefactor of the magazine at a time when it had fallen on hard times.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-33) In 1955, [George Kirstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Kirstein "George Kirstein") replaced Freda Kirchway as magazine owner.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-34)[James J. Storrow Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_J._Storrow_Jr. "James J. Storrow Jr.") bought the magazine from Kirstein in 1965.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-35)

### 1970s to 2024

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1970s to 2024")]

See also: [Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation_Magazine_v._United_States_Department_of_Defense "Nation Magazine v. United States Department of Defense")

On the eve of the 1968 U.S. presidential election the magazine argued that the choice between Nixon and Humphrey was such a bad one that voters should stay home.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-36) In June 1979, _The Nation_'s publisher [Hamilton Fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Fish_V "Hamilton Fish V") moved the magazine to 72 [Fifth Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Avenue "Fifth Avenue"), in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:2-4)_The Nation's_ current address is 33 Irving Place in New York.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-37)

In 1977, a group organized by [Hamilton Fish V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Fish_V "Hamilton Fish V") bought the magazine from the Storrow family.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-38) In 1985, the magazine was sold to for undiscosed amount to "The Nation Co", headed by millionaire Arthur Carter and two former owners of _The Nation_.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:0-39)

In March 1991, _The Nation_ together with [Center for Constitutional Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_for_Constitutional_Rights "Center for Constitutional Rights") sued [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") for allegedly violating First Amendment and Fifth Amendment for creating [press pools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_pool "Press pool") during [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War"). Judge [Leonard B. Sand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_B._Sand "Leonard B. Sand") ruled the case [moot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mootness "Mootness").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-40) In 1995, veteran editor [Victor Navasky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Navasky "Victor Navasky") and a group of investors that included [Paul Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Newman "Paul Newman") acquired the magazine. Navasky became the magazine's publisher and editorial director.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-41) In 1995, [Katrina vanden Heuvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katrina_vanden_Heuvel "Katrina vanden Heuvel") succeeded Navasky as editor of _The Nation._[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-42) In 2005, she became the magazine's editor and publisher.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-43)

> "In an era of instant, 140-character news cycles and reflexive toeing of the party line, it's incredible to think of the 150-year history of The Nation. It's more than a magazine - it's a crucible of ideas forged in the time of Emancipation, tempered through depression and war and the civil-rights movement, and honed as sharp and relevant as ever in an age of breathtaking technological and economic change."

—[Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"),per _[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")_[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:obama-44)

In 2015, _The Nation_ celebrated its 150th anniversary with a documentary film by Academy Award–winning director [Barbara Kopple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Kopple "Barbara Kopple"), which analyzed the magazine's history.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-45)_The Nation_ also held a celebration in [St. Ann's Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Ann's_Warehouse "St. Ann's Warehouse") in Brooklyn, which was attended by [Tony Kushner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Kushner "Tony Kushner"), [Bill de Blasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_de_Blasio "Bill de Blasio"), [Walter Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Mosley "Walter Mosley") and [Michael Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moore "Michael Moore").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-46) To mark the anniversary, former US President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") wrote a letter praising _The Nation_ but noting that he disagreed with some of the magazine's views.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:obama-44) Editor of _The Nation_, [D. D. Guttenplan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._D._Guttenplan "D. D. Guttenplan") wrote a biography of the magazine entitled _The Nation: A Biography (The First 150 Years)_. [History News Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_News_Network "History News Network") said that the biography "has played, and continues to play, an important role in U.S. history, society, and politics".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-47)

In January 2016, _The Nation_ endorsed [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont")[Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate")[Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") for [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") for the third time in its history. The editorial board professed; "Voters can trust Sanders because he doesn't owe his political career to the financial overlords of the status quo. Freed from these chains of special interest, he can take the bold measures that the country needs".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-48) On June 15, 2019, Heuvel stepped down as editor; D. D. Guttenplan, the editor-at-large, took her place.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-june2019-49)

On February 23, 2022, _The Nation_ named _[Jacobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobin\_(magazine) "Jacobin (magazine)")_ founder [Bhaskar Sunkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaskar_Sunkara "Bhaskar Sunkara") its new president. In an interview, Sunkara said that he believes [liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States") and [socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism "Socialism") need to form a coalition to ensure progress and him becoming a president of _The Nation_ was one way towards this goal.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:5-7) In December 2023, Sunkara announced the magazine would be switching from a biweekly format to a larger monthly publication.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3)

## Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Finances")]

Print ad pages declined by 5% from 2009 to 2010, while [digital advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_advertising "Digital advertising") rose 32.8% from 2009 to 2010.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-50) Advertising accounts for 10% of total revenue for the magazine, while circulation totals 60%.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-NYT1-51)_The Nation_ has lost money in all but three or four years of operation and is sustained in part by a group of more than 30,000 donors called Nation Associates, who donate funds to the periodical above and beyond their annual subscription fees. This program accounts for 30% of the total revenue for the magazine. An annual cruise also generates $200,000 for the magazine.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-NYT1-51) Since late 2012, the Nation Associates program has been called Nation Builders.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-52)

In 2023, the magazine had approximately 91,000 subscribers, roughly 80% of whom pay for the print magazine. Adding sales from newsstands, _The Nation_ had a total circulation of 96,000 copies per issue in 2021, earning the majority of its revenue from subscriptions and donations, rather than print advertising.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-:1-3)

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Poetry")]

Since its creation, _The Nation_ has published significant works of [American poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_poetry "American poetry"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54) including works by [Hart Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hart_Crane "Hart Crane"), [Eli Siegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Siegel "Eli Siegel"), [Elizabeth Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bishop "Elizabeth Bishop"), and [Adrienne Rich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Rich "Adrienne Rich"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53) as well as [W. S. Merwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._S._Merwin "W. S. Merwin"), [Pablo Neruda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Neruda "Pablo Neruda"), [Denise Levertov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_Levertov "Denise Levertov"), and [Derek Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Walcott "Derek Walcott").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54)

In 2018, the magazine published a poem entitled "How-To" by Anders Carlson-Wee which was written in the voice of a homeless man and used [black vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Vernacular_English "African-American Vernacular English"). This led to criticism from writers such as [Roxane Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxane_Gay "Roxane Gay") because Carlson-Wee is white. _The Nation_'s two poetry editors, [Stephanie Burt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Burt "Stephanie Burt") and [Carmen Giménez Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Gim%C3%A9nez_Smith "Carmen Giménez Smith"), issued an apology for publishing the poem, the first such action ever taken by the magazine.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53) The apology itself became an object of criticism also. Poet and _Nation_ columnist [Katha Pollitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katha_Pollitt "Katha Pollitt") called the apology "craven" and likened it to a letter written from "a reeducation camp".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schuessler-53)[Grace Schulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Schulman "Grace Schulman"), _The Nation_'s poetry editor from 1971 to 2006, wrote that the apology represented a disturbing departure from the magazine's traditionally broad conception of [artistic freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_freedom "Artistic freedom").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Schulman-54)

## Regular columns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Nation&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Regular columns")]

The magazine runs a number of regular columns:

*   "Beneath the Radar" by [Gary Younge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Younge "Gary Younge")
*   "Deadline Poet" by [Calvin Trillin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Trillin "Calvin Trillin")
*   "Diary of a Mad Law Professor" by [Patricia J. Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_J._Williams "Patricia J. Williams")
*   "The Liberal Media" by [Eric Alterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Alterman "Eric Alterman")
*   "Subject to Debate" by [Katha Pollitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katha_Pollitt "Katha Pollitt")
*   "Between the Lines" by [Laila Lalami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laila_Lalami "Laila Lalami")

Regular columns in the past have included:

*   "Look Out" by [Naomi Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_Klein "Naomi Klein")
*   "Sister Citizen" by [Melissa Harris-Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melissa_Harris-Perry "Melissa Harris-Perry")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-55)
*   "Beat the Devil" (1984–2012) by [Alexander Cockburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Cockburn "Alexander Cockburn")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-56)
*   "Dispatches" (1984–87) by [Max Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Holland "Max Holland") and Kai Bird[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-Hiar-57)
*   "Minority Report" (1982–2002) by [Christopher Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hitchens "Christopher Hitchens")
*   "The Nation [cryptic crossword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptic_crossword "Cryptic crossword")" by [Frank W. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_W._Lewis "Frank W. Lewis") from 1947 to 2009, and Joshua Kosman and Henri Picciotto from 2011 to 2020, that is now available by subscription[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nation_(magazine)#cite_note-58)

The **University of Chicago** (**UChicago**, **Chicago**, **UChi,** or **U of C**) is a [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university "Private university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_Chicago "Hyde Park, Chicago") community area of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"), Illinois, United States.

The university is composed of an [undergraduate college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_the_University_of_Chicago "College of the University of Chicago") and four graduate research divisions: the Arts & Humanities Division, the Biological Sciences Division, the Physical Sciences Division, and the Social Sciences Division, all of which include various organized departments and institutes. In addition, the university operates seven professional schools in the fields of [business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Booth_School_of_Business "University of Chicago Booth School of Business"), [social work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Family_School_of_Social_Work,_Policy,_and_Practice "Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice"), [theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Divinity_School "University of Chicago Divinity School"), [public policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Harris_School_of_Public_Policy "University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy"), [law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Law_School "University of Chicago Law School"), [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_School_of_Medicine "Pritzker School of Medicine"), and [molecular engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_School_of_Molecular_Engineering "Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering"), along with a school of [continuing studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_School_of_Continuing_Liberal_and_Professional_Studies "Graham School of Continuing Liberal and Professional Studies"). The university maintains an [overseas campus in Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Hong_Kong "University of Chicago Hong Kong"), as well as academic centers in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), [Luxor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxor "Luxor"), and downtown Chicago.

University of Chicago scholars have played a role in the development of many academic disciplines, including economics, law, literary criticism, mathematics, physics, religion, sociology, and political science, establishing the [Chicago schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_school_(disambiguation) "Chicago school (disambiguation)") of thought in various fields. The university's [Metallurgical Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallurgical_Laboratory "Metallurgical Laboratory") produced the world's first human-made, self-sustaining nuclear reaction in [Chicago Pile-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Pile-1 "Chicago Pile-1") beneath the viewing stands of the university's [Stagg Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagg_Field "Stagg Field"). Advances in chemistry led to the "radiocarbon revolution" in the [carbon-14 dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating "Radiocarbon dating") of ancient life and objects. The university operates and administers research institutions including [Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermilab "Fermilab") and [Argonne National Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonne_National_Laboratory "Argonne National Laboratory"). The [University of Chicago Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Press "University of Chicago Press") is the largest [university press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_university_presses "List of university presses") in North America.

As of 2025, the university's students, faculty, and staff have included [101 Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_by_university_affiliation "List of Nobel laureates by university affiliation"). The university's [faculty members and alumni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_University_of_Chicago_people "List of University of Chicago people") also include 11 [Fields Medalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_Medal "Fields Medal"), 4 [Turing Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award") winners, 2 [Dan David Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_David_Prize "Dan David Prize") winners, 58 [MacArthur Fellows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows_Program "MacArthur Fellows Program"), 30 [Marshall Scholars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Scholars "Marshall Scholars"), 56 [Rhodes Scholars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship"), 29 [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") winners, 20 [National Humanities Medalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Humanities_Medal "National Humanities Medal"), and 6 [Olympic medalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_universities_with_Olympic_medals "List of American universities with Olympic medals").

## History
