**Richard Stanton Lambert** (25 August 1894 – 27 November 1981) was an English [biographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographer "Biographer"), popular historian and broadcaster. He was also the founding editor of [_The Listener_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Listener_(magazine) "The Listener (magazine)") and an employee of the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") and [CBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Canadian Broadcasting Corporation"). His books mainly concern history and biography but he also wrote about crime, travel, art, radio, film and propaganda. In _Ariel and All His Quality_ he wrote about his time with the BBC in its formative years. _Propaganda_, published in 1939, was a timely investigation of a subject already made familiar during World War I.

For _Franklin of the Arctic: a life of adventure_, published by [McClelland and Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McClelland_and_Stewart "McClelland and Stewart") in 1949, Lambert won both the first [Governor General's Award for Juvenile Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General's_Award_for_Juvenile_Fiction "Governor General's Award for Juvenile Fiction") and the third [Canadian Library Association Book of the Year for Children Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Library_Association_Book_of_the_Year_for_Children_Award "Canadian Library Association Book of the Year for Children Award").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-ogwc-GG-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-winners-CLA-2)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_S._Lambert&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Lambert was born in Kingston upon Thames, England, and was the son of [Richard Cornthwaite Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cornthwaite_Lambert "Richard Cornthwaite Lambert") a barrister and [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK) "Liberal Party (UK)") politician.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-obit-3) He was educated at [Repton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repton_School "Repton School") and [Wadham College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadham_College,_Oxford "Wadham College, Oxford"), where he studied Classics. Some of his poems were published in the Oxford University literary magazine _[Oxford Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford\_Poetry "Oxford Poetry")_, then in its formative years. After leaving Oxford, he worked as a sub-editor with _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ from 1914–1915, joining the staff in 1916.

During World War I, he served with the [Friends' Ambulance Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends'_Ambulance_Unit "Friends' Ambulance Unit") (FAU), from 1916–1918. In a 1971 retrospective, he records that he was a C.O. ([conscientious objector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscientious_objector "Conscientious objector")), to which fact he ascribed a difficulty in finding a job in the post-war years. However, he found part-time work at Sheffield University teaching economics and history to extramural groups of Yorkshire miners and railwaymen. This work left him free during the summer to pursue his literary work.

In 1918, Lambert married Kate Elinor Klein, a talented artist and wood engraver who signed herself Elinor Lambert. They established [The Stanton Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stanton_Press "The Stanton Press") together in 1921, producing fine, hand-printed volumes of poetry and translation. The press closed in 1924 when Lambert took up a full-time post as a tutor for the University of London.

In 1927, he joined the BBC as Head of the Adult Education Section and, in 1928, he became the first editor of _[The Listener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Listener\_(magazine) "The Listener (magazine)")_ magazine. At this time the magazine was intended primarily to disseminate talks delivered by the BBC. Under Lambert's editorship notable contributors to _The Listener_ included members of the Bloomsbury Group [Paul Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nash_(artist) "Paul Nash (artist)"), [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry") and [Clive Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Bell "Clive Bell").

In April 1939, R.S. Lambert resigned from the BBC and migrated to Canada with his family. There he joined [CBC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBC_Radio "CBC Radio"), being named educational advisor in 1940. His collections of wartime broadcasts for CBC were published in several volumes.

In 1944, he divorced Kate Elinor Lambert and married Joyce Morgan.

From 1943 to 1959 he served CBC as Supervisor of School Broadcasts, retiring in 1963 to live in a neo-Gothic rectory called Claverleigh at Creemore (now called [Clearview, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearview,_Ontario "Clearview, Ontario")). Always a prolific author, he continued to write books in his retirement about the history of Canada and Canadian folklore and legend. He died on 27 November 1981 at the [Royal Jubilee Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Jubilee_Hospital "Royal Jubilee Hospital"), [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia"), [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-Times_Colonist_28_November_1981-4) In 1990, Claverleigh was designated a [National Historic Site of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Sites_of_Canada "National Historic Sites of Canada").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-5)

## Paranormal interests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_S._Lambert&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Paranormal interests")]

Lambert was interested in the supernatural as a hobby throughout his life and wrote two books on the subject. The first, published in 1935, was entitled _The Haunting of Cashen's Gap_. The second book, entitled _Exploring the Supernatural_, was the first significant study of supernatural occurrences in Canada.

The first book was about the phenomenon of [Gef the talking mongoose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gef_the_talking_mongoose "Gef the talking mongoose"). The mongoose was said to be haunting an isolated farmhouse on the Isle of Man. Lambert accompanied his friend, paranormal investigator [Harry Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Price "Harry Price") and together they wrote the book. Lambert's apparent credulity about the talking mongoose led [Sir Cecil Levita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Levita "Cecil Levita") to criticise him, suggesting that he was unfit to serve on the Board of the [British Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute"), of which Lambert was one of the founders and a prominent Governor in the 1930s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-6) Levita said that Lambert was "off his head" because he had believed in the talking mongoose and the [evil eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_eye "Evil eye"). Lambert sued Levita for slander. Lambert was pressured to abandon his action by [Sir Stephen Tallents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Tallents "Stephen Tallents") but persisted with it and won, receiving £7,600 in damages, then an exceptional figure for a slander case, awarded because Lambert's counsel managed to introduce a BBC memo which showed Lambert's career had been threatened if he persisted with the case. The case became known as "The Mongoose Case".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-8)

The case achieved wide media coverage in the popular press of the day. It had important repercussions for Lambert's employer, the BBC, as well as for the British Film Institute.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Richard Stanton Lambert** (25 August 1894 – 27 November 1981) was an English [biographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographer "Biographer"), popular historian and broadcaster. He was also the founding editor of [_The Listener_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Listener_(magazine) "The Listener (magazine)") and an employee of the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") and [CBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Canadian Broadcasting Corporation"). His books mainly concern history and biography but he also wrote about crime, travel, art, radio, film and propaganda. In _Ariel and All His Quality_ he wrote about his time with the BBC in its formative years. _Propaganda_, published in 1939, was a timely investigation of a subject already made familiar during World War I.

For _Franklin of the Arctic: a life of adventure_, published by [McClelland and Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McClelland_and_Stewart "McClelland and Stewart") in 1949, Lambert won both the first [Governor General's Award for Juvenile Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General's_Award_for_Juvenile_Fiction "Governor General's Award for Juvenile Fiction") and the third [Canadian Library Association Book of the Year for Children Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Library_Association_Book_of_the_Year_for_Children_Award "Canadian Library Association Book of the Year for Children Award").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-ogwc-GG-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-winners-CLA-2)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_S._Lambert&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Lambert was born in Kingston upon Thames, England, and was the son of [Richard Cornthwaite Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Cornthwaite_Lambert "Richard Cornthwaite Lambert") a barrister and [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK) "Liberal Party (UK)") politician.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-obit-3) He was educated at [Repton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repton_School "Repton School") and [Wadham College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadham_College,_Oxford "Wadham College, Oxford"), where he studied Classics. Some of his poems were published in the Oxford University literary magazine _[Oxford Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford\_Poetry "Oxford Poetry")_, then in its formative years. After leaving Oxford, he worked as a sub-editor with _[The Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Economist "The Economist")_ from 1914–1915, joining the staff in 1916.

During World War I, he served with the [Friends' Ambulance Unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friends'_Ambulance_Unit "Friends' Ambulance Unit") (FAU), from 1916–1918. In a 1971 retrospective, he records that he was a C.O. ([conscientious objector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscientious_objector "Conscientious objector")), to which fact he ascribed a difficulty in finding a job in the post-war years. However, he found part-time work at Sheffield University teaching economics and history to extramural groups of Yorkshire miners and railwaymen. This work left him free during the summer to pursue his literary work.

In 1918, Lambert married Kate Elinor Klein, a talented artist and wood engraver who signed herself Elinor Lambert. They established [The Stanton Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stanton_Press "The Stanton Press") together in 1921, producing fine, hand-printed volumes of poetry and translation. The press closed in 1924 when Lambert took up a full-time post as a tutor for the University of London.

In 1927, he joined the BBC as Head of the Adult Education Section and, in 1928, he became the first editor of _[The Listener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Listener\_(magazine) "The Listener (magazine)")_ magazine. At this time the magazine was intended primarily to disseminate talks delivered by the BBC. Under Lambert's editorship notable contributors to _The Listener_ included members of the Bloomsbury Group [Paul Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nash_(artist) "Paul Nash (artist)"), [Roger Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Fry "Roger Fry") and [Clive Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Bell "Clive Bell").

In April 1939, R.S. Lambert resigned from the BBC and migrated to Canada with his family. There he joined [CBC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBC_Radio "CBC Radio"), being named educational advisor in 1940. His collections of wartime broadcasts for CBC were published in several volumes.

In 1944, he divorced Kate Elinor Lambert and married Joyce Morgan.

From 1943 to 1959 he served CBC as Supervisor of School Broadcasts, retiring in 1963 to live in a neo-Gothic rectory called Claverleigh at Creemore (now called [Clearview, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearview,_Ontario "Clearview, Ontario")). Always a prolific author, he continued to write books in his retirement about the history of Canada and Canadian folklore and legend. He died on 27 November 1981 at the [Royal Jubilee Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Jubilee_Hospital "Royal Jubilee Hospital"), [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia"), [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-Times_Colonist_28_November_1981-4) In 1990, Claverleigh was designated a [National Historic Site of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Historic_Sites_of_Canada "National Historic Sites of Canada").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-5)

## Paranormal interests

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Richard_S._Lambert&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Paranormal interests")]

Lambert was interested in the supernatural as a hobby throughout his life and wrote two books on the subject. The first, published in 1935, was entitled _The Haunting of Cashen's Gap_. The second book, entitled _Exploring the Supernatural_, was the first significant study of supernatural occurrences in Canada.

The first book was about the phenomenon of [Gef the talking mongoose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gef_the_talking_mongoose "Gef the talking mongoose"). The mongoose was said to be haunting an isolated farmhouse on the Isle of Man. Lambert accompanied his friend, paranormal investigator [Harry Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Price "Harry Price") and together they wrote the book. Lambert's apparent credulity about the talking mongoose led [Sir Cecil Levita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Levita "Cecil Levita") to criticise him, suggesting that he was unfit to serve on the Board of the [British Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute"), of which Lambert was one of the founders and a prominent Governor in the 1930s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-6) Levita said that Lambert was "off his head" because he had believed in the talking mongoose and the [evil eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil_eye "Evil eye"). Lambert sued Levita for slander. Lambert was pressured to abandon his action by [Sir Stephen Tallents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Tallents "Stephen Tallents") but persisted with it and won, receiving £7,600 in damages, then an exceptional figure for a slander case, awarded because Lambert's counsel managed to introduce a BBC memo which showed Lambert's career had been threatened if he persisted with the case. The case became known as "The Mongoose Case".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_S._Lambert#cite_note-8)

The case achieved wide media coverage in the popular press of the day. It had important repercussions for Lambert's employer, the BBC, as well as for the British Film Institute.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Henry Louis Mencken** (September 12, 1880 – January 29, 1956) was an American [journalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalist "Journalist"), [essayist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essayist "Essayist"), [satirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satirist "Satirist"), [cultural critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_critic "Cultural critic"), and scholar of [American English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-WVobit-1) He commented widely on literature, music, prominent politicians, and contemporary movements. His satirical reporting on the [Scopes trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopes_trial "Scopes trial"), which he dubbed the "Monkey Trial", also earned him attention. The term _[Menckenian](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Menckenian "wikt:Menckenian")_ has entered multiple [dictionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictionaries "Dictionaries") to describe anything of or pertaining to Mencken, including his combative [rhetorical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhetoric "Rhetoric") and [prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose "Prose") styles.

As a scholar, Mencken is known for _[The American Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_American\_Language "The American Language")_, a multi-volume study of how the English language is spoken in the United States. As an admirer of the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany")[philosopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosopher "Philosopher")[Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche "Friedrich Nietzsche"), he was an outspoken opponent of [organized religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organized_religion "Organized religion"), [theism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theism "Theism"), [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship "Censorship"), [populism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populism "Populism"), [Prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition "Prohibition"), and [representative democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy "Representative democracy"), the last of which he once defined as "the worship of jackals by jackasses".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-American_Tricksters-2) Mencken was a supporter of [scientific progress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_progress "Scientific progress") and was critical of [osteopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteopathy "Osteopathy") and [chiropractic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractic "Chiropractic"). He was also an open critic of [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics").

Mencken opposed the [American entry into World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_entry_into_World_War_I "American entry into World War I") and [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_entry_into_World_War_II "American entry into World War II"). Some of the opinions in his private diary entries have been described by some researchers as [racist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_the_United_States "Racism in the United States") and [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitic "Antisemitic"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-latimes1989-3) although this characterization has been disputed. [Larry S. Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_S._Gibson "Larry S. Gibson") argued that Mencken's views on race changed significantly between his early and later private writings which started when he was 50, and that it was more accurate to describe Mencken as elitist rather than racist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-gibson-4) He seemed to show a genuine enthusiasm for [militarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Militarism "Militarism") but never in its American form. "War is a good thing," he wrote, "because it is honest; it admits the central fact of human nature... A nation too long at peace becomes a sort of gigantic old maid."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-5)

His longtime home in the [Union Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Square,_Baltimore "Union Square, Baltimore") neighborhood of [West Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Baltimore "West Baltimore") was turned into a city museum, the [H. L. Mencken House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken_House "H. L. Mencken House"). His papers were distributed among various city and university libraries, with the largest collection held in the Mencken Room at the central branch of Baltimore's [Enoch Pratt Free Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enoch_Pratt_Free_Library "Enoch Pratt Free Library").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Mencken was born in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), on September 12, 1880. He was the son of Anna Margaret (Abhau) and [August Mencken Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Mencken_Sr. "August Mencken Sr."), a [cigar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cigar "Cigar") factory owner. He was of [German ancestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_American "German American") and spoke [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") in his childhood.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-7) When Henry was three, his family moved into a new home at 1524 Hollins Street facing Union Square park in the [Union Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Square,_Baltimore "Union Square, Baltimore") neighborhood of old West Baltimore. Apart from five years residing elsewhere during the marriage that left him a widower in middle age, Mencken would stay there for the rest of his life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-8)

In his bestselling memoir _[Happy Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy\_Days,\_1880%E2%80%931892 "Happy Days, 1880–1892")_, he described his childhood in Baltimore as "placid, secure, uneventful and happy".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-9)

When he was nine years old, he read [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain "Mark Twain")'s _[Huckleberry Finn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures\_of\_Huckleberry\_Finn "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn")_, which he later described as "the most stupendous event in my life".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-10) He became determined to become a writer and read voraciously. In one winter while in high school he read [William Makepeace Thackeray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Makepeace_Thackeray "William Makepeace Thackeray") and then "proceeded backward to [Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Addison "Joseph Addison"), [Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Steele "Richard Steele"), [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope "Alexander Pope"), [Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swift "Jonathan Swift"), [Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Johnson "Samuel Johnson") and the other magnificos of the Eighteenth century". He read the entire canon of [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare "Shakespeare") and became an ardent fan of [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling") and [Thomas Huxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Huxley "Thomas Huxley").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldberg192590%E2%80%9393-11) As a boy, Mencken also had practical interests, [photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photography "Photography") and [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry") in particular, and eventually had a home chemistry [laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory "Laboratory") in which he performed experiments of his own design, some of them inadvertently dangerous.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-12)

He began his primary education in the mid-1880s at Professor Knapp's School on the east side of Holliday Street between East Lexington and Fayette Streets, next to the [Holliday Street Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holliday_Street_Theatre "Holliday Street Theatre") and across from the newly constructed [Baltimore City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_City_Hall "Baltimore City Hall"). The site today is the [War Memorial and City Hall Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Memorial_Plaza "War Memorial Plaza") laid out in 1926 in memory of World War I dead. At 15, in June 1896, he graduated as valedictorian from the [Baltimore Polytechnic Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_Polytechnic_Institute "Baltimore Polytechnic Institute"), at the time a males-only mathematics, technical and science-oriented [public high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_high_school "Public high school").

He worked for three years in his father's cigar factory. He disliked the work, especially the sales aspect of it, and resolved to leave, with or without his father's blessing. In early 1898 he took a writing class at the Cosmopolitan University,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldberg192593-13) a free correspondence school established by [The Cosmopolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitan_(magazine) "Cosmopolitan (magazine)") magazine.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-14) This was to be the entirety of Mencken's formal [post-secondary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-secondary_education "Post-secondary education") in journalism, or in any other subject. Upon his father's death a few days after Christmas in the same year, the business passed to his uncle, and Mencken was free to pursue his career in journalism. He applied in February 1899 to the _Morning Herald_ newspaper (which became the _[Baltimore Morning Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore\_Morning\_Herald "Baltimore Morning Herald")_ in 1900) and was hired part-time, but still kept his position at the factory for a few months. In June he was hired as a full-time reporter.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/H._L._Mencken_-_The_Borzoi_Cropped_Retouched.jpg/250px-H._L._Mencken_-_The_Borzoi_Cropped_Retouched.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H._L._Mencken_-_The_Borzoi_Cropped_Retouched.jpg)

Mencken c.1920

Mencken served as a reporter at the _Herald_ for six years. Fewer than two-and-a-half years after the [Great Baltimore Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Baltimore_Fire "Great Baltimore Fire"), the paper was purchased in June 1906 by [Charles H. Grasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_H._Grasty "Charles H. Grasty"), the owner and editor of _[The News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore\_News-American "Baltimore News-American")_ since 1892 and competing owner and publisher Gen. [Felix Agnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Agnus "Felix Agnus"), of the town's oldest (since 1773) and largest daily, _[The Baltimore American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Baltimore\_American "The Baltimore American")._ They proceeded to divide the staff, assets and resources of _The Herald_ between them. Mencken then moved to _[The Baltimore Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Baltimore\_Sun "The Baltimore Sun")_, where he worked for Charles H. Grasty. He continued to contribute to _The Sun,_ _The Evening Sun_ (founded 1910) and _The Sunday Sun_ full-time until 1948, when he stopped writing after suffering a stroke.

Mencken began writing the editorials and opinion pieces that made his name at _The Sun._ On the side, he wrote short stories, a novel, and even poetry, which he later revealed. In 1908, he became a literary critic for _[The Smart Set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Smart\_Set "The Smart Set")_ magazine, and in 1924 he and [George Jean Nathan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Jean_Nathan "George Jean Nathan") founded and edited _[The American Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_American\_Mercury "The American Mercury")_, published by [Alfred A. Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf "Alfred A. Knopf"). It soon developed a national circulation and became highly influential on college campuses across America. In 1933, Mencken resigned as editor.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/H_L_Mencken_Carl_Van_Vechten.jpg/250px-H_L_Mencken_Carl_Van_Vechten.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H_L_Mencken_Carl_Van_Vechten.jpg)

Mencken photographed by [Carl Van Vechten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Van_Vechten "Carl Van Vechten"), 1932

During the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), Mencken did not support the [New Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal "New Deal"), which cost him popularity. In 1931, the [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas") legislature passed a motion to pray for Mencken's soul after he had called the state the "apex of moronia".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-15) In the mid-1930s, Mencken feared President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") and his [New Deal liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Deal_liberalism "New Deal liberalism") as a powerful force. Mencken was "deeply conservative, resentful of change, looking back upon the 'happy days' of a bygone time, wanted no part of the world that the New Deal promised to bring in" according to Charles A. Fecher.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-16) Mencken had strong reservations regarding US participation in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). He ceased writing for _The Baltimore Sun_ for several years, focusing on his memoirs and other projects as editor while he served as an adviser for the paper that had been his home for nearly his entire career.

In 1948, he briefly returned to the political scene to cover the presidential election in which President [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") faced [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")[Thomas Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dewey "Thomas Dewey") and [Henry A. Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_A._Wallace "Henry A. Wallace") of the [Progressive Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_Party_(United_States,_1948) "Progressive Party (United States, 1948)"). His later work consisted of humorous, anecdotal, and nostalgic essays that were first published in _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ and then collected in the books _Happy Days_, _Newspaper Days_, and _Heathen Days_.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/Sara_Haardt.jpg/250px-Sara_Haardt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sara_Haardt.jpg)

[Sara Haardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Haardt "Sara Haardt") Mencken

Mencken cultivated a public persona of a contented bachelor, but he did ultimately have long-term relationships with two women. The first was the writer and nurse [Marion Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Bloom "Marion Bloom"), whom he met around 1914. They had an on-and-off romantic relationship for about a decade. Their correspondence (later published) makes clear it was a genuine love affair, though Mencken ultimately did not marry her, which caused her considerable heartbreak.

On August 27, 1930, Mencken married [Sara Haardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Haardt "Sara Haardt"), a [German American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_American "German American") professor of English at [Goucher College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goucher_College "Goucher College") in Baltimore and an author eighteen years his junior.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-17) Haardt had led an unsuccessful effort in [Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama "Alabama") to ratify the [19th Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") supporting women's suffrage.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-19) The two met in 1923, after Mencken delivered a lecture at Goucher; a seven-year courtship ensued. The marriage made national headlines, and many were surprised that Mencken, who once called marriage "the end of hope" and who was well known for mocking relations between the sexes, had gone to the altar. "The [Holy Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit "Holy Spirit") informed and inspired me", Mencken said. "Like all other infidels, I am superstitious and always follow hunches: this one seemed to be a superb one."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-20) Even more startling, he was marrying an Alabama native, despite his having written scathing essays about the [American South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_South "American South"). Haardt was in poor health from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis") throughout their marriage and died in 1935 of [meningitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meningitis "Meningitis"), leaving Mencken grief-stricken.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-21) He had always championed her writing, and after her death, had a collection of her short stories published under the title _Southern Album_. Haardt's childhood friend the Alabama author [Sara Mayfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Mayfield "Sara Mayfield") wrote extensively about Haardt and Mencken in her 1968 book _The Constant Circle: H. L. Mencken and His Friends_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-22)

### Last years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Last years")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/H.L._Mencken_by_A._Aubrey_Bodine.jpg/250px-H.L._Mencken_by_A._Aubrey_Bodine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H.L._Mencken_by_A._Aubrey_Bodine.jpg)

Mencken photographed on his 75th birthday by [A. Aubrey Bodine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Aubrey_Bodine "A. Aubrey Bodine")

On November 23, 1948, Mencken suffered a stroke, which left him aware and fully conscious but nearly unable to read or write and able to speak only with difficulty. After his stroke, Mencken enjoyed listening to classical music, and after some recovery of his ability to speak, talking with friends, but he sometimes referred to himself in the past tense, as if he were already dead. During the last year of his life, his friend and biographer [William Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Manchester "William Manchester") read to him daily.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-23)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Death")]

Mencken died in his sleep on January 29, 1956.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-25) He was interred in Baltimore's [Loudon Park Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudon_Park_Cemetery "Loudon Park Cemetery").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-26) A very small, short, and private service was held, in accordance with Mencken's wishes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-27)

Although it does not appear on his tombstone, Mencken, during his _Smart Set_ days, wrote a joking epitaph for himself:

> If, after I depart this vale, you ever remember me and have thought to please my ghost, forgive some sinner and wink your eye at some homely girl.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-28)

In his capacity as editor, Mencken became close friends with the leading literary figures of his time, including [Theodore Dreiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Dreiser "Theodore Dreiser"), [F.Scott Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._Scott_Fitzgerald "F. Scott Fitzgerald"), [Joseph Hergesheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Hergesheimer "Joseph Hergesheimer"), [Anita Loos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Loos "Anita Loos"), [Ben Hecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Hecht "Ben Hecht"), [Sinclair Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinclair_Lewis "Sinclair Lewis"), [James Branch Cabell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Branch_Cabell "James Branch Cabell"), and [Alfred Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf_Sr. "Alfred A. Knopf Sr."), as well as a mentor to several young reporters, including [Alistair Cooke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alistair_Cooke "Alistair Cooke"). He also championed artists whose works he considered worthy. For example, he asserted that books such as _Caught Short! A Saga of Wailing Wall Street_ (1929), by [Eddie Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Cantor "Eddie Cantor") (ghostwritten by [David Freedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Freedman "David Freedman")) did more to pull America out of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") than all government measures combined. He also mentored [John Fante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fante "John Fante"). [Thomas Hart Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hart_Benton_(painter) "Thomas Hart Benton (painter)") illustrated an edition of Mencken's book _Europe After 8:15_.

Mencken also published many works under various pseudonyms, including [Owen Hatteras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Hatteras "Owen Hatteras"), John H Brownell, William Drayham, WLD Bell, and [Charles Angoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Angoff "Charles Angoff").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-29) As a ghostwriter for the physician [Leonard K. Hirshberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_K._Hirshberg "Leonard K. Hirshberg"), he wrote a series of articles, and in 1910, most of a book about the care of babies.

Mencken was an outspoken critic of [Prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prohibition "Prohibition"). His detestation of the Eighteenth Amendment aligned Mencken with the cultural elite of his time. He led intellectual and emotional campaigns to eradicate Prohibition and went as far to vote for [Franklin Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Roosevelt "Franklin Roosevelt") in 1932 to accomplish this abolition of the Eighteenth Amendment. Mencken viewed the freedom to drink as critical liberty and considered alcohol as one of humanity's greatest inventions.

Mencken admired the German philosopher [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche "Friedrich Nietzsche") (he was the first writer to provide a scholarly analysis in English of Nietzsche's views and writings) and [Joseph Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Conrad "Joseph Conrad"). His humor and satire owed much to [Ambrose Bierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose_Bierce "Ambrose Bierce") and [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain "Mark Twain"). He did much to defend Theodore Dreiser despite freely admitting his faults, including stating forthrightly that Dreiser often wrote badly and was gullible. Mencken expressed his appreciation for [William Graham Sumner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Graham_Sumner "William Graham Sumner") in a 1941 collection of Sumner's essays and regretted never having known him. Mencken was scathing in his criticism of the German philosopher [Hans Vaihinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Vaihinger "Hans Vaihinger"), whom Mencken described as "an extremely dull author" and whose famous book _Philosophy of 'As If'_ he dismissed as an unimportant "foot-note to all existing systems".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-30)

Mencken recommended for publication philosopher and author [Ayn Rand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayn_Rand "Ayn Rand")'s first novel, _[We the Living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We\_the\_Living "We the Living")_ and called it "a really excellent piece of work". Shortly afterwards, Rand addressed him in correspondence as "the greatest representative of a philosophy" to which she wanted to dedicate her life, "individualism", and later listed him as her favorite columnist.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-31)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/ae/Inherit333-1.JPG/250px-Inherit333-1.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Inherit333-1.JPG)

Mencken is fictionalized in the play _[Inherit the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inherit\_the\_Wind\_(play) "Inherit the Wind (play)")_ (a fictionalized version of the [Scopes monkey trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopes_trial "Scopes trial") of 1925) as the cynical sarcastic atheist E.K. Hornbeck (right), seen here as played by [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") in the [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_(film_industry) "Hollywood (film industry)")[film version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inherit_the_Wind_(1960_film) "Inherit the Wind (1960 film)"). On the left is Henry Drummond, based on [Clarence Darrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Darrow "Clarence Darrow") and portrayed by [Spencer Tracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Tracy "Spencer Tracy").

For Mencken, _[Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures\_of\_Huckleberry\_Finn "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn")_ was the finest work of [American literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_literature "American literature"). He particularly relished Mark Twain's depiction of a succession of gullible and ignorant townspeople, "boobs", as Mencken referred to them, who are repeatedly gulled by a pair of colorful [con men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Con_men "Con men"): the deliberately pathetic ["Duke" and "Dauphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures_of_Huckleberry_Finn#The_Duke_and_the_Dauphin "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn")", with whom [Huck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huckleberry_Finn "Huckleberry Finn") and [Jim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_(Huckleberry_Finn) "Jim (Huckleberry Finn)") travel down the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"). For Mencken, the depiction epitomizes the hilarious dark side of America, where democracy, as defined by Mencken, is "the worship of jackals by jackasses".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-American_Tricksters-2)

Such turns of phrase evoked the erudite cynicism and rapier sharpness of language displayed by [Ambrose Bierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambrose_Bierce "Ambrose Bierce") in his darkly satiric _[The Devil's Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Devil's\_Dictionary "The Devil's Dictionary")_. A noted curmudgeon, democratic in subjects attacked, Mencken savaged politics, hypocrisy, and social convention.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-LAT-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-33) A master of English, he was given to bombast and once disdained the lowly hot dog bun's descent into "the soggy rolls prevailing today, of ground acorns, plaster of Paris, flecks of bath sponge and atmospheric air all compact".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-34)

Defining [Puritanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritanism "Puritanism") as "the haunting fear that someone, somewhere, may be happy", Mencken believed that the US had not cast aside the Puritans' influence.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Fitzpatrick-35) He opined that American culture, unlike its European counterparts, had not attained intellectual freedom, and judged literature by moral orthodoxy and not by artistic merit.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Fitzpatrick-35) His most outspoken essay was "Puritanism as a Literary Force" from his 1917 collection of essays _[A Book of Prefaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Book\_of\_Prefaces "A Book of Prefaces")_:

> The Puritan's utter lack of aesthetic sense, his distrust of all romantic emotion, his unmatchable intolerance of opposition, his unbreakable belief in his own bleak and narrow views, his savage cruelty of attack, his lust for relentless and barbarous persecution – these things have put an almost unbearable burden up on the exchange of ideas in the United States.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-36)

As a nationally syndicated [columnist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicated_columnist "Syndicated columnist") and book author, he commented widely on the social scene, literature, music, prominent politicians and contemporary movements, such as the temperance movement. Mencken was a keen cheerleader of scientific progress, skeptical of economic theories and strongly opposed to [osteopathic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteopathic "Osteopathic")/[chiropractic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractic "Chiropractic") medicine. He also debunked the idea of objective news reporting since "truth is a commodity that the masses of undifferentiated men cannot be induced to buy" and added a humorous description of how "Homo Boobus", like "higher mammalia", is moved by "whatever gratifies his prevailing yearnings".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-37)

As a frank admirer of Nietzsche, Mencken was a detractor of [representative democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy "Representative democracy"), which he believed was a system in which inferior men dominated their superiors.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Democracy-38) Also, like Nietzsche, Mencken lambasted [religious belief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_belief "Religious belief") and the very concept of God, as he was an unflinching [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist"). He was particularly hostile to [Christian fundamentalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_fundamentalism "Christian fundamentalism"), [Christian Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Science "Christian Science") and [creationism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creationism "Creationism"), and towards the "Booboisie", his word for the ignorant middle classes.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Keating-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-prejudices-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Whorton-41) In the summer of 1925 he attended the famous Scopes "Monkey Trial" in Dayton, Tennessee, and wrote scathing columns for the _Baltimore Sun_ (these widely syndicated) and _American Mercury_ mocking the [anti-evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-evolution "Anti-evolution") fundamentalists (especially [William Jennings Bryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jennings_Bryan "William Jennings Bryan")). The play _[Inherit the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inherit\_the\_Wind\_(play) "Inherit the Wind (play)")_ is a fictional version of the trial, and as noted above the cynical reporter E.K. Hornbeck is based on Mencken. In 1926, he deliberately had himself arrested for selling an issue of _The American Mercury_, which was [banned in Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banned_in_Boston "Banned in Boston") by the [Comstock laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comstock_laws "Comstock laws").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-42) Mencken heaped scorn not only on the public officials he disliked but also on the state of American elective politics.

In the summer of 1926, Mencken followed with great interest the Los Angeles grand jury inquiry into the famous Canadian American evangelist [Aimee Semple McPherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Semple_McPherson "Aimee Semple McPherson"). She was accused of faking her reported [kidnapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidnapping "Kidnapping") and the case attracted national attention. There was every expectation that Mencken would continue his previous pattern of anti-fundamentalist articles, this time with a searing critique of McPherson. Unexpectedly, he came to her defense by identifying various local religious and civic groups that were using the case as an opportunity to pursue their respective ideological agendas against the embattled [Pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostal "Pentecostal") minister.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-43) He spent several weeks in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"), California, and wrote many scathing and satirical columns on the movie industry and [Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_California "Southern California") culture. After all charges had been dropped against McPherson, Mencken revisited the case in 1930 with a sarcastic and observant article. He wrote that since many of that town's residents had acquired their ideas "of the true, the good and the beautiful" from the movies and newspapers, "Los Angeles will remember the testimony against her long after it forgets the testimony that cleared her".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-44)

### Science and mathematics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Science and mathematics")]

Mencken defended the evolutionary views of [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin") but spoke unfavorably of many prominent physicists and had little regard for pure mathematics. Regarding [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics "Theoretical physics"), he said to longtime editor [Charles Angoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Angoff "Charles Angoff"), "Imagine measuring infinity! That's a laugh."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Angoff,_Charles_1961_pp._141-45) Elsewhere, he dismissed higher mathematics and [probability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory "Probability theory") as "nonsense", after he read Angoff's article for [Charles Sanders Peirce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sanders_Peirce "Charles Sanders Peirce") in the _American Mercury_: "So you believe in that garbage, too—theories of knowledge, infinity, laws of probability. I can make no sense of it, and I don't believe you can either, and I don't think your god Peirce knew what he was talking about."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-46)

Mencken repeatedly identified mathematics with metaphysics and theology. According to Mencken, mathematics is necessarily infected with metaphysics. Mathematicians tend to engage in metaphysical speculation. In a review of [Alfred North Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead")'s _The Aims of Education,_ Mencken remarked that, although he agreed with Whitehead's thesis and admired his writing style, "Now and then he falls into mathematical jargon and pollutes his discourse with equations", and "[T]here are moments when he seems to be following some of his mathematical colleagues into the gaudy metaphysics which now entertains them".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-47) For Mencken, theology was characterized by it using correct reasoning from false premises. Mencken uses the term "theology" more generally to refer to the use of logic in science or any field of knowledge. In a review of [Arthur Eddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Eddington "Arthur Eddington")'s _The Nature of the Physical World_ and [Joseph Needham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Needham "Joseph Needham")'s _[Man a Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man\_a\_Machine "Man a Machine")_, Mencken ridiculed the use of reasoning to establish any fact in science.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-48)

Mencken wrote a review of Sir [James Jeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Jeans "James Jeans")'s book, _The Mysterious Universe_, in which Mencken wrote that mathematics is not necessary for physics. Instead of mathematical "speculation" (such as [quantum theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics "Quantum mechanics")), Mencken believed physicists should directly look at individual facts in the laboratory, as do chemists.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Mencken_252%E2%80%9354-49)

In the same article, which he re-printed in the _Mencken [Chrestomathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrestomathy "Chrestomathy"),_ Mencken primarily contrasts what real scientists do, which is to simply directly look at the existence of "shapes and forces" confronting them instead of (such as in statistics) attempting to speculate and use mathematical models. Physicists and especially astronomers are consequently not real scientists, because when looking at shapes or forces, they do not simply "patiently wait for further light", but resort to mathematical theory. There is no need for statistics in scientific physics, since one should simply look at the facts while statistics attempts to construct mathematical models. On the other hand, the really competent physicists do not bother with the "theology" or reasoning of mathematical theories (such as in quantum mechanics).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-Mencken_252%E2%80%9354-49)

Mencken ridiculed [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein "Albert Einstein")'s theory of [general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity"), believing that "in the long run his curved space may be classed with the [psychosemantic bumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrenology "Phrenology") of [Gall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Joseph_Gall "Franz Joseph Gall") and [Spurzheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spurzheim "Spurzheim")".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-50)

### Race and elitism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Race and elitism")]

In addition to his identification of races with castes, Mencken had views about the superior individual within communities. He believed that every community produced a few people of clear superiority. He considered groupings on a par with hierarchies, which led to a kind of natural [elitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elitism "Elitism") and natural [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy"). "Superior" individuals, in Mencken's view, were those wrongly oppressed and disdained by their own communities but nevertheless distinguished by their will and personal achievement, not by race or birth. In 1989, following his instructions, Alfred A. Knopf published Mencken's "secret diary" as _The Diary of H.L. Mencken_. According to an Associated Press story, Mencken's views shocked even the "sympathetic scholar who edited it", [Charles Fecher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Fecher "Charles Fecher") of Baltimore.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-latimes1989-3) A club in Baltimore, the [Maryland Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_Club "Maryland Club"), had one Jewish member. When that member died, Mencken said, "There is no other Jew in Baltimore who seems suitable." The diary also quoted him as saying of his black maid, in September 1943, that "it is impossible to talk anything resembling discretion or judgment to a colored woman. They are all essentially child-like, and even hard experience does not teach them anything".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-51)

Mencken opposed [lynching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching_in_the_United_States "Lynching in the United States"). In 1935, he testified before Congress in support of the [Costigan–Wagner Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costigan%E2%80%93Wagner_Bill "Costigan–Wagner Bill"). While he had previously written negatively about lynchings during the 1910s and 1920s, the lynchings of [Matthew Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching_of_Matthew_Williams "Lynching of Matthew Williams") and [George Armwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Armwood "George Armwood") caused him to write in support of the bill and give political advice to [Walter White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_White_(NAACP) "Walter White (NAACP)") on how to maximize the likelihood of the bill's passing.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-olson8-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-53) The two lynchings in his home state made the issue directly relevant to him. His arguments against lynching were influenced by his interpretation of civilization, as he believed that a civilized society would not tolerate it.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-olson8-52)

One of his biographers observed that:

> ... he was receptive to black writers, without question more helpful than any other editor of his time. Both [W.E.B. Du Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W.E.B._Du_Bois "W.E.B. Du Bois") and the poet [Countee Cullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countee_Cullen "Countee Cullen") appeared in the _Mercury's_ pages during its first year, and in later issues poets [James Weldon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Weldon_Johnson "James Weldon Johnson") and [Langston Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langston_Hughes "Langston Hughes") and future NAACP head [Walter F. White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_F._White "Walter F. White") were represented. The black journalist [George Schuyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Schuyler "George Schuyler"), who contributed nine essays to the _Mercury,_ was to appear more frequently in the magazine in the final six years of Mencken's editorship than any other writer.

—Fred Hobson[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-54)

In a review of _The Skeptic: A Life of H. L. Mencken_, by [Terry Teachout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Teachout "Terry Teachout"), journalist [Christopher Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hitchens "Christopher Hitchens") described Mencken as a [German nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_nationalist "German nationalist"), "an antihumanist as much as an atheist", who was "prone to the hyperbole and [sensationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensationalism "Sensationalism") he distrusted in others". Hitchens also criticized Mencken for writing a scathing critique of [Franklin Delano Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Delano_Roosevelt "Franklin Delano Roosevelt") but nothing equally negative of [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-55)

[Larry S. Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_S._Gibson "Larry S. Gibson") argued that Mencken's views on race changed significantly between his early and later writings, attributing some of the changes in Mencken's views to his experience of being treated as an outsider due to his German heritage during World War I. Gibson speculated that much of Mencken's language was intended to lure in readers by suggesting a shared negative view of other races, and then writing about their positive aspects. Describing Mencken as elitist rather than racist, he says Mencken ultimately believed that humans consisted of a small group of those of superior intelligence and a mass of inferior people, regardless of race.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-gibson-4)

Mencken scholar Marion Elizabeth Rodgers has argued that, despite the racial slurs and ethnic slang in the diaries, Mencken rebelled against "the Aryan imbecilities of Hitler" and stated: "To me personally, race prejudice is one of the most preposterous of all the imbecilities of mankind. There are so few people on earth worth knowing that I hate to think of any man I like as a German or a Frenchman, a gentile or a Jew, Negro or a white man."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-56)

#### Anglo-Saxons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Anglo-Saxons")]

Mencken countered the arguments for Anglo-Saxon superiority prevalent in his time in a 1923 essay entitled "The Anglo-Saxon", which argued that if there was such a thing as a pure "Anglo-Saxon" race, it was defined by its inferiority and cowardice: "The normal American of the 'pure-blooded' majority goes to rest every night with an uneasy feeling that there is a burglar under the bed and he gets up every morning with a sickening fear that his underwear has been stolen."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-57)

#### Jews

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Jews")]

[Chaz Bufe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaz_Bufe "Chaz Bufe"), an admirer of Mencken, wrote that Mencken's various antisemitic statements should be understood in the context that Mencken made bombastic and over-the-top denunciations of almost any national, religious, and ethnic group. One of his autobiographers noted:

> Thus, rhetorically at least, he lived life more dramatically than most other mortals, attempted more, risked more, said more, and said it more colorfully on a wider range of subjects than perhaps any other writer of his generation. The result, depending on what he came out with at any given time, was that he appeared to be both the best friend and the worst enemy of Jews, blacks, and numerous other segments of the population. The truth is that a hundred statements could be chosen to "prove" Mencken anti-Semitic and a hundred to "prove" he was not.

—Fred Hobson[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-58)

That said, Bufe still wrote that some of Mencken's statements were "odious", such as his claim in his 1918 introduction to Nietzsche's [_The Anti-Christ_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Antichrist_(book) "The Antichrist (book)") that "The case against the Jews is long and damning; it would justify ten thousand times as many [pogroms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pogrom "Pogrom") as now go on in the world".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-59) Mencken was also an Axis sympathizer who berated the Allied war effort as late as 1944.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-60)

Historian [David T. Beito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_T._Beito "David T. Beito") points out that Mencken often showed greater sensitivity toward the suffering of Jews than most other leading figures during the period, including [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt"). In January 1939 Mencken proposed immediate admission to the U.S. of all the German Jews. There was "no reason whatsoever for believing it would be impossible to absorb them, or even difficult." Mencken pointed out that "Almost as many Jews as that came into the United States during every year from 1903 to 1914, and yet the republic somehow survived." He considered it unfair to expect American Jews to carry the funding burden because it would only make them targets of the "Ku Kluxers". He challenged the "so-called Christians... who are now so free with weasel words of comfort and flattery, and so curiously stingy with practical aid" to take financial responsibility.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-61)

## Memorials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Memorials")]

### Home

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Home")]

Mencken's home at 1524 Hollins Street in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore")'s [Union Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Square,_Baltimore "Union Square, Baltimore") neighborhood, where he lived for 67 years, was bequeathed to the [University of Maryland, Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland,_Baltimore "University of Maryland, Baltimore") on the death of his younger brother, August, in 1967. The City of Baltimore acquired the property in 1983, and the [H. L. Mencken House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken_House "H. L. Mencken House") became part of the City Life Museums. The house was restored in 2019, with the third floor and rear of the second floor becoming the headquarters of the Baltimore National Heritage Area. The first floor and front of the second floor appear much as they were in the 1940s, and constitute the H. L. Mencken House Museum, overseen by the nonprofit Society to Preserve H. L. Mencken's Legacy. It is opened for special events, and individual and group visits are available by arrangement.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-62)

### Papers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=H._L._Mencken&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Papers")]

Shortly after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Mencken expressed his intention of bequeathing his books and papers to Baltimore's [Enoch Pratt Free Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enoch_Pratt_Free_Library "Enoch Pratt Free Library"). At his death, it was in possession of most of the present large collection. As a result, his papers as well as much of his personal library, which includes many books inscribed by major authors, are held in the Library's Central Branch on Cathedral Street in Baltimore. The original third floor _H.L. Mencken Room and Collection_ housing this collection was dedicated on April 17, 1956.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-schmidt87-63) The new Mencken Room, on the first floor of the Library's Annex, was opened in November 2003.

The collection contains Mencken's typescripts, newspaper and magazine contributions, published books, family documents and memorabilia, clipping books, large collection of presentation volumes, file of correspondence with prominent Marylanders, and the extensive material he collected while he was preparing _[The American Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_American\_Language "The American Language")_.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-schmidt87-63)

Other Mencken related collections of note are at [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"), [Johns Hopkins University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University"), and [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"). In 2007, Johns Hopkins acquired "nearly 6,000 books, photographs and letters by and about Mencken" from "the estate of an Ohio accountant".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-64)

The Sara Haardt Mencken collection at [Goucher College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goucher_College "Goucher College") includes letters exchanged between Haardt and Mencken and condolences written after her death. Some of Mencken's vast literary correspondence is held at the [New York Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library"). "Gift of HL Mencken 1929" is stamped on _[The Marriage of Heaven and Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Marriage\_of\_Heaven\_and\_Hell "The Marriage of Heaven and Hell")_, Luce 1906 edition of [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake"), which shows up from the Library of Congress online version for reading. Mencken's letters to Louise (Lou) Wylie, a reporter and feature writer for New Orleans's _[The Times-Picayune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times-Picayune "The Times-Picayune")_ newspaper, are archived at [Loyola University New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_University_New_Orleans "Loyola University New Orleans").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._L._Mencken#cite_note-65)
